cases.title: Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa
cases.facts:
The appellant Board fined some of its employees for misconduct. The employees filed a claim before
the Labour Court. The Board raised a preliminary objection that it was a statutory body performing
sovereign/civic functions and not an 'industry' under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act
(IDA), 1947, hence the Labour Court had no jurisdiction.
cases.issues:
1. What is the precise definition and scope of 'Industry' under Section 2(j) of the IDA?
2. Do statutory bodies, hospitals, educational institutions, and charitable organizations fall
within the ambit of 'industry'?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The Board argued it performed regal and civic functions (water supply/sewerage) without any profit
motive. It was not a trade, business, or manufacture, and thus fell outside the IDA.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The workmen argued that 'industry' must be interpreted broadly to fulfill the IDA 's objective of
resolving disputes. The nature of the activity, not the motive of the employer, determines if it is an
industry.
cases.judgment:
Result: A 7-judge Constitution Bench formulated the 'Triple Test' and vastly expanded the definition
of industry, ruling against the Board.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Krishna Iyer established the 'Triple Test': An activity is an industry if there is (1) Systematic
activity, (2) Organized by cooperation between employer and employee, (3) For the production and/
or distribution of goods and services calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes. The Court ruled
that absence of profit motive is irrelevant. Hospitals, educational institutions, clubs, and research
institutes are industries if they pass this test. Only strict sovereign functions (legislative, judicial,
police) are excluded.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Established the 'Triple Test' for defining an industry.
2. Profit motive or capital investment is not essential.
3. Sovereign functions are excluded, but civic/welfare functions of the state are included.

cases.title: Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL) v. National Union Waterfront Workers
cases.facts:
Various public sector undertakings, including SAIL, engaged contract labour. The Central
Government issued notifications under Section 10(1) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and
Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA) abolishing contract labour in certain operations. Following abolition, the
contract workers demanded automatic absorption/regularization as direct employees of the
principal employer (SAIL).
cases.issues:
1. Does the abolition of contract labour under Section 10 of the CLRA automatically result in the
absorption of the contract workers by the principal employer?
2. Can the Industrial Tribunal order such absorption?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
SAIL argued that the CLRA Act is silent on absorption. Section 10 only prohibits contract labour; it
does not mandate the creation of an employment contract between the principal employer and the
displaced workers.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The Unions relied on the ' Air India Statutory Corp' judgment, arguing that upon abolition, the
intermediary contractor vanishes, and a direct relationship between the principal employer and
workmen automatically springs up to prevent mass unemployment.
cases.judgment:
Result: A 5-judge Constitution Bench overruled the ' Air India' judgment, holding that there is no
automatic absorption of contract labour upon abolition.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that neither Section 10 nor any other provision of the CLRA implies automatic
absorption. The legislature deliberately omitted such a provision. However, the Court clarified two
crucial exceptions: If the contract is found to be a 'sham' or 'camouflage' (where the principal
employer actually controls the workers), the tribunal can pierce the veil and declare them direct
employees. Second, if the principal employer intends to employ regular workers for the abolished
processes, preference must be given to the displaced contract workers.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Abolition of contract labour under the CLRA does not lead to automatic absorption.
2. Tribunals can order absorption only if the contract is proven to be a sham/camouflage.
3. Displaced workers have preferential rights for future regular employment.

cases.title: Excel Wear v. Union of India
cases.facts:
Excel Wear, a registered partnership firm, faced severe labor unrest, violence, and indiscipline,
making it impossible to run the factory. They applied for prior permission from the State
Government to close down the undertaking under Section 25-O of the IDA. The Government
arbitrarily refused permission. The employer challenged the constitutional validity of Section 25-O.
cases.issues:
1. Is Section 25-O of the Industrial Disputes Act, which mandates prior government permission
for closing down a business, violative of the fundamental right to carry on trade or business
under Article 19(1)(g)?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The employer argued that the right to carry on a business includes the right to close it down. Forcing
an employer to run a business incurring losses or facing severe violence is an unreasonable restriction
under Article 19(6).
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The Union of India argued that Section 25-O was enacted in the interest of the general public to
prevent mass unemployment and protect workmen from whimsical closures.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court struck down Section 25-O (as it then stood) as unconstitutional, ruling in
favor of the employer.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the right to close down a business is an integral part of the fundamental right to
carry on a business under Article 19(1)(g). The original Section 25-O gave unchecked, arbitrary power
to the government to refuse permission without requiring any reasons, without any time limit, and
without any appellate remedy. Forcing an employer to continue running a dead or dangerous
business is highly unreasonable. (Note: Following this, Parliament amended Section 25-O to cure
these defects by adding time limits, hearing requirements, and review mechanisms).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The right to close down a business is a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g).
2. Restrictions on closure must be reasonable, providing for fair hearings and objective reasons.
3. Absolute, unguided administrative power to block business closures is unconstitutional.

cases.title: People's Union for Democratic Rights (PUDR) v. Union of India (Asiad Workers Case)
cases.facts:
PUDR, an NGO, filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) alleging severe labor law violations during the
construction of facilities for the 1982 Asian Games in Delhi. Contractors were employing workmen
through 'jamadars' (middlemen) who deducted a cut from the workers' wages, resulting in workers
receiving far less than the statutory minimum wage. Children were also employed in hazardous
construction.
cases.issues:
1. Can a third party (NGO) file a writ petition on behalf of marginalized workers under Article
32?
2. Does payment of wages below the statutory minimum wage amount to 'forced labour' violating
Article 23 of the Constitution?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
PUDR argued that extracting labor for less than the minimum wage violates human dignity and
amounts to forced labor (begar) prohibited under Article 23.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The Union of India argued PUDR had no locus standi. Further, they argued 'forced labor' only means
physical or legal coercion, not economic compulsion where a worker 'voluntarily' accepts lower
wages.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court recognized PUDR's locus standi and delivered a landmark ruling
expanding the definition of 'forced labor'.
cases.reasoning:
Justice P .N. Bhagwati revolutionized PILs, holding that when the poor/illiterate cannot approach the
court, any public-spirited body can file a writ on their behalf. Critically, the Court expanded Article
23. It held that 'force' is not just physical or legal force; it includes economic compulsion. When a
person is destitute and forced by hunger and poverty to accept wages lower than the minimum wage,
they are providing 'forced labor'. Therefore, paying less than the minimum wage is a direct violation
of the fundamental right against exploitation under Article 23.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Locus standi is relaxed for PILs advocating for marginalized classes.
2. Payment of wages below the statutory minimum wage constitutes 'forced labor' under Article
23.
3. Economic compulsion is a recognized form of coercion.

cases.title: State Bank of India v. N. Sundara Money
cases.facts:
N. Sundara Money was appointed as a temporary cashier in SBI for a fixed period. His appointment
order explicitly stated his employment would automatically terminate on a specific date without any
notice. When the date arrived, his services were terminated. He challenged this, claiming he had
worked for more than 240 days and his termination amounted to 'retrenchment' under Section 2(oo)
of the IDA. Since he wasn't paid retrenchment compensation under Section 25F, he argued the
termination was illegal.
cases.issues:
1. Does the termination of employment by the efflux of a fixed-term contract amount to
'retrenchment' under Section 2(oo) of the IDA?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The workman argued that 'retrenchment' means the termination of service 'for any reason
whatsoever' (excluding voluntary retirement, superannuation, or ill health). Expiration of a contract is
not explicitly excluded, so it must be retrenchment.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
SBI argued that this was an automatic cessation of work based on an agreed contract. There was no
positive act of 'termination' by the employer, hence no retrenchment.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the workman, holding that termination by the expiry of
a fixed-term contract was indeed retrenchment.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Krishna Iyer applied a strict literal interpretation to Section 2(oo). The phrase 'for any reason
whatsoever' is extraordinarily broad. It covers every form of termination that does not fall into the
specifically listed exceptions. At the time, the expiration of a fixed-term contract was not one of the
exceptions. Therefore, the employer's act of ending the employment, even as per the contract,
constituted retrenchment. Since the mandatory condition precedent (Section 25F compensation) was
not fulfilled, the termination was void. (Note: This judgment caused a massive uproar, leading the
Parliament to amend the IDA in 1984, inserting clause (bb) to Section 2(oo) to exclude fixed-term
contracts from the definition of retrenchment)..
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. 'Retrenchment' covers termination of service for any reason whatsoever, unless explicitly
excepted.
2. Triggered the legislative insertion of Section 2(oo)(bb) to exclude fixed-term contracts.
3. Non-compliance with Section 25F renders retrenchment void ab initio.

cases.title: Workmen of M/s Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co. of India P. Ltd. v. The Management
cases.facts:
Prior to 1971, if an employer conducted a proper domestic enquiry into a workman's misconduct and
dismissed him, the Industrial Tribunal had no power to interfere with the punishment unless there
was victimization or unfair labor practice. To cure this, Parliament enacted Section 11A of the IDA,
empowering Tribunals to review the evidence and alter the punishment. Firestone dismissed several
workmen after a domestic enquiry. The workmen appealed to the Tribunal under the newly enacted
Section 11A.
cases.issues:
1. What is the scope of the Tribunal's power under Section 11A of the IDA?
2. Can the Tribunal re-appraise the evidence produced in the domestic enquiry and substitute its
own penalty?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The workmen argued that Section 11A makes the Tribunal an appellate authority. It has the plenary
power to review facts, re-weigh evidence, and decide if the dismissal was proportionate to the
misconduct.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The management argued that Section 11A did not destroy the employer's managerial prerogative. If
the domestic enquiry was fair, the Tribunal should not interfere.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court upheld the broad powers of the Tribunal under Section 11A,
fundamentally changing Indian disciplinary jurisprudence.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that Section 11A completely altered the law. The Tribunal now has both the right and
the duty to appraise the evidence itself to satisfy itself whether the misconduct is proved.
Furthermore, even if the misconduct is proved, the Tribunal has the power to decide whether the
punishment of dismissal is shockingly disproportionate to the offense. It can set aside the dismissal
and award a lesser punishment (like withholding increments) or direct reinstatement. The Tribunal
sits as an appellate court over the employer's domestic enquiry.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 11A grants appellate powers to Industrial Tribunals over domestic disciplinary
enquiries.
2. Tribunals can re-appraise evidence and determine the proportionality of the punishment.
3. Protects workmen from arbitrary or excessively harsh dismissals.

cases.title: T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu
cases.facts:
In 2003, over two lakh government employees in Tamil Nadu went on an unprecedented strike to
protest the reduction of pension benefits. Invoking the Tamil Nadu Essential Services Maintenance
Act (TESMA) and conduct rules, the State Government summarily dismissed all 2,00,000 striking
employees overnight without holding any individual enquiries. The employees challenged the
dismissals, arguing they had a right to strike.
cases.issues:
1. Do government employees have a fundamental, statutory, or moral right to strike?
2. Was the en masse dismissal of 2 lakh employees legally valid?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The employees argued that the right to strike is an inherent part of collective bargaining and the right
to form associations under Article 19(1)(c). They also argued the mass dismissals violated principles
of natural justice (Article 311).
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The State argued that government servants are bound by conduct rules that explicitly prohibit strikes.
A strike by state machinery paralyses society.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court strongly condemned the strike, ruling that government employees have
no fundamental or statutory right to strike, but intervened on humanitarian grounds to reinstate
most employees.
cases.reasoning:
The Court declared unequivocally that government employees hold a special status. They have no
fundamental right to strike under Article 19. Furthermore, there is no statutory or moral right to
strike. Society suffers immensely when government machinery halts. The Court observed that
employees have alternative mechanisms (Tribunals, Courts) to air grievances. However, regarding the
mass dismissals, the Court found the State's action draconian. Using its equitable powers, the Court
directed the State to reinstate all employees who were not involved in violence, while upholding the
punishment for the strike leaders.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Government employees have absolutely no fundamental, statutory, or equitable right to strike.
2. Strikes by civil servants are illegal and violate conduct rules.
3. Mass dismissals without individual hearings violate natural justice, necessitating equitable
intervention.

cases.title: Syndicate Bank v. K. Umesh Nayak
cases.facts:
Bank employees went on strike to press for their demands. The management deducted wages for the
days the employees were on strike, applying the principle of 'no work, no pay'. The unions challenged
this deduction before the tribunals, which resulted in conflicting judgments from various High
Courts on whether workers are entitled to wages during a strike.
cases.issues:
1. Are workmen entitled to wages for the period they go on strike?
2. What is the legal distinction between a 'legal' strike and a 'justified' strike?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The union argued that striking is a legitimate weapon of collective bargaining. If the strike is peaceful
and launched for valid grievances, denying wages amounts to penalizing them for exercising their
labor rights.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The Bank argued that wages are consideration for work done. If workers refuse to work, the employer
is under no obligation to pay them ('no work, no pay').
cases.judgment:
Result: A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court ruled that workmen are entitled to wages only if
the strike is BOTH legal and justified.
cases.reasoning:
The Court resolved the conflict by holding that the right to strike is a statutory right under the IDA,
but it is heavily regulated. The Court established a conjunctive test: For workers to claim wages for
the strike period, the strike must be both legal (in compliance with Sections 22 and 23 of the IDA
regarding notice periods and conciliation pendency) AND justified (the demands must be reasonable
and not taken for frivolous reasons). If a strike is illegal (even if justified) or unjustified (even if legal),
the workers are not entitled to wages. The principle of 'no work, no pay' applies unless both
conditions are met.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. General rule during a strike is 'no work, no pay'.
2. Wages are payable only if the strike is BOTH legally compliant and factually justified.
3. An illegal strike can never be justified.

cases.title: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
cases.facts:
Bandhua Mukti Morcha, an NGO, sent a letter to the Supreme Court alleging the existence of a
massive bonded labor system in the stone quarries of Faridabad (Haryana). The workers were living
in sub-human conditions, subjected to forced labor to pay off generational debts, without clean water,
medical facilities, or minimum wages. The letter was treated as a writ petition under Article 32.
cases.issues:
1. Is the existence of bonded labor a violation of Article 21 (Right to Life) and Article 23 (Right
against Exploitation)?
2. What is the State's duty in identifying, releasing, and rehabilitating bonded laborers under the
Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The petitioner argued that the State was turning a blind eye to modern-day slavery. They argued that
Right to Life under Article 21 includes the right to live with human dignity.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The State of Haryana raised a preliminary objection, arguing the petition was based on a mere letter
and lacked proper affidavits. They also claimed these were voluntary contract workers, not bonded
laborers.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court heavily criticized the State government, issued 21 sweeping directives for
the release and rehabilitation of the workers, and expanded Article 21.
cases.reasoning:
Justice P .N. Bhagwati brushed aside technical objections regarding the format of the PIL. He held that
Article 21 guarantees the right to live with human dignity, free from exploitation. The Court laid
down a legal presumption: if any worker is providing labor and is denied the minimum wage, the
Court will presume they are a bonded laborer extracting forced labor under a debt obligation,
shifting the burden of proof to the employer/State to prove otherwise. The Court mandated that the
State has a constitutional obligation not just to free them, but to rehabilitate them so they don't fall
back into slavery.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right to Life (Article 21) includes the right to live with human dignity, free from bonded
labor.
2. Procedural technicalities cannot block Article 32 petitions concerning gross human rights
violations.
3. Presumption of bonded labor arises if a worker is paid less than the minimum wage.

cases.title: H.R. Adyanthaya v. Sandoz (India) Ltd.
cases.facts:
Medical Representatives (Promotion and Sales Representatives) working for various pharmaceutical
companies raised industrial disputes regarding their service conditions and terminations. The
employers raised a preliminary objection that Medical Representatives do not fall under the
definition of 'workman' under Section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, and therefore the labor
courts had no jurisdiction.
cases.issues:
1. Are Medical/Sales Representatives 'workmen' under Section 2(s) of the IDA?
2. What is the criteria for classifying an employee as a workman?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The employees argued that their work involved significant clerical and manual effort (carrying
sample bags, writing daily reports). Since they didn't have managerial/supervisory powers, they
should be classified as workmen.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The employers argued that their primary job was sales promotion, negotiating, and canvassing
doctors. Clerical duties were purely incidental. Therefore, they did not fit into any of the operational
categories mentioned in Section 2(s).
cases.judgment:
Result: A 5-judge Constitution Bench ruled that Medical Representatives are NOT 'workmen' under
the Industrial Disputes Act.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly analyzed Section 2(s), which defines a workman as any person employed to do any
manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work. The Court held that to
be a workman, the employee must strictly fall into one of these specific categories. The primary duty
of a Medical Representative is sales promotion and canvassing, which requires intellect and
persuasion. This is neither manual, clerical, technical, nor supervisory. Even though they write
reports (clerical) or carry bags (manual), these are merely incidental to their main work of sales.
Therefore, they fall outside the ambit of the IDA. (Note: They are covered separately under the Sales
Promotion Employees (Conditions of Service) Act, 1976).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. To be a 'workman' under Section 2(s) IDA, the employee must perform work that is primarily
manual, clerical, technical, operational, or supervisory.
2. Sales promotion and canvassing do not fall into these categories.
3. Incidental clerical or manual duties do not convert a sales role into a workman role.

cases.title: Christian Medical College Hospital Employees' Union v. CMC Vellore Association
cases.facts:
CMC Vellore, a reputed minority educational and medical institution, dismissed several employees
for indiscipline. The Employees' Union raised an industrial dispute. The management challenged the
application of the Industrial Disputes Act to their institution. They argued that being a minority
institution, they had a fundamental right under Article 30(1) to establish and administer the
institution without state interference, which included absolute disciplinary control over their staff.
cases.issues:
1. Does the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, apply to minority educational institutions?
2. Does the application of labor laws (like Section 11A) infringe upon the fundamental right of
minorities to administer their institutions under Article 30(1)?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The Union argued that Article 30(1) is not a charter for exploitation. General regulatory laws aimed at
social welfare and industrial peace apply equally to all employers.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The Management argued that allowing Industrial Tribunals to reinstate dismissed staff or interfere
with their disciplinary decisions completely destroys their administrative autonomy guaranteed by
Article 30(1).
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court ruled that the Industrial Disputes Act applies uniformly to minority
institutions and does not violate Article 30(1).
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the right to administer under Article 30(1) does not mean the right to
maladminister or exploit labor. The IDA is a general, secular law designed to maintain industrial
peace, prevent unfair labor practices, and protect workers from arbitrary dismissal. These laws act as
reasonable regulations necessary for the healthy operation of any institution. Subjecting a minority
institution to the scrutiny of a Labour Court ensures fairness and does not destroy its minority
character or educational objectives. The fundamental right to religion/minority status cannot be used
as a shield against national labor legislations.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Minority institutions under Article 30(1) are fully subject to the Industrial Disputes Act.
2. Labor welfare legislations are general regulatory measures that do not infringe on minority
administrative autonomy.
3. The right to administer is subject to reasonable regulations preventing maladministration.

cases.title: Standard Vacuum Refining Co. v. Its Workmen
cases.facts:
The workmen of Standard Vacuum Refining Co. demanded a higher bonus, arguing that despite the
company's massive profits, the wages paid to them were far below the 'living wage' standard. The
company argued it was already paying wages higher than the industry average and the minimum
wage, and therefore should not be forced to distribute more profits as a bonus to bridge the gap to a
living wage.
cases.issues:
1. What is the distinction between a Minimum Wage, a Fair Wage, and a Living Wage?
2. Are workmen entitled to a bonus if their actual wages fall short of a 'living wage' despite the
employer's high profitability?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The workmen argued that Article 43 of the Constitution directs the State to secure a 'living wage'.
Since their current wages merely covered basic necessities and not a decent standard of life, the
surplus profits should be shared to bridge this gap.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The management argued that 'living wage' is a utopian concept. They argued that bonus is an ex-
gratia payment and cannot be demanded as a right to continuously increase wages.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the workmen, laying down the foundational definitions
of wage structures in Indian labor law.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Gajendragadkar defined the three tiers of wages: (1) Minimum Wage: The absolute bare
minimum for physical subsistence of the worker and their family; it must be paid regardless of the
company's financial capacity. (2) Fair Wage: Above minimum wage, below living wage; depends on
the employer's capacity to pay and industry standards. (3) Living Wage: The highest standard,
providing not just bare essentials, but also education, healthcare, insurance, and a decent measure of
frugal comfort. The Court held that since the company was highly prosperous and the workers' wages
had not yet reached the 'living wage' standard, they were entitled to a bonus from the surplus profits
to help bridge that gap.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Established the tripartite classification of wages: Minimum, Fair, and Living Wage.
2. Minimum wage must be paid regardless of the employer's capacity to pay.
3. Bonus is not a charity but a mechanism to bridge the gap between actual wages and the living
wage.

cases.title: Crown Aluminium Works v. Their Workmen
cases.facts:
Due to financial difficulties and a slump in the market, the management of Crown Aluminium Works
unilaterally revised the wages and dearness allowance of its workmen downwards. The workmen
raised an industrial dispute. The management argued that just as wages are revised upwards when
the company makes profits, they have the inherent right to revise wages downwards to save the
industry from collapsing during financial distress.
cases.issues:
1. Can an employer unilaterally revise the wage structure downwards to the detriment of the
workmen?
2. What are the limits on downward revision of wages under industrial law?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The workmen argued that a downward revision destroys their standard of living. Wages, once fixed
by agreement or award, cannot be reduced, as they are mostly at subsistence levels anyway.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The management argued that an inflexible wage structure would lead to the closure of the factory,
resulting in total unemployment, which is worse than a pay cut.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court ruled that while downward revision is theoretically possible, it cannot be
allowed to fall below the minimum wage level.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established a crucial protection for labor. It held that an employer cannot reduce wages
below the 'bare minimum wage' under any circumstances. If an industry cannot pay the bare
minimum wage to its workers, it has no right to exist. However, if the industry is paying a 'fair wage'
or 'living wage' (which is higher than the minimum), and it faces severe, persistent financial distress,
a downward revision might be permissible as a last resort to save the industry from closure. But this
cannot be done arbitrarily; it must be through negotiation or tribunal adjudication, proving genuine
financial incapacity.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Wages cannot be reduced below the statutory 'bare minimum wage' under any financial
distress.
2. If an employer cannot pay the minimum wage, they have no right to run the business.
3. Downward revision of 'fair wages' is highly restricted and permissible only in extreme
financial crises to prevent closure.

cases.title: Sanjit Roy v. State of Rajasthan
cases.facts:
The State of Rajasthan experienced severe drought and famine. The State Government initiated public
works under the Rajasthan Famine Relief Works Employees (Exemption from Labour Laws) Act,
1964. Under this Act, the government exempted these relief works from the Minimum Wages Act,
paying the drought-stricken villagers significantly less than the statutory minimum wage, arguing it
was 'relief work' and not normal employment.
cases.issues:
1. Does the exemption of famine relief works from the Minimum Wages Act violate Article 23
(Right against Exploitation)?
2. Can the State pay less than minimum wage under the guise of providing 'relief' or 'charity'?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The petitioner argued, relying on the PUDR (Asiad) case, that any labor extracted for less than the
minimum wage is forced labor (begar). Exploiting the misery of famine-stricken people by paying
them starvation wages is unconstitutional.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The State argued that famine relief is not commercial employment. It is a welfare measure to provide
at least some sustenance to people who would otherwise starve. Paying full minimum wages would
deplete relief funds, helping fewer people.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court struck down the Exemption Act, ruling that the State must pay the
minimum wage even for famine relief work.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Bhagwati emphatically held that the State cannot act as an exploiter. When the State employs a
person, even for famine relief, it must pay the minimum wage. The Court reiterated that extracting
labor for less than minimum wage from a person driven by poverty and hunger falls squarely under
'forced labor' prohibited by Article 23. The State's argument that it is providing 'help' is invalid; true
help respects human dignity, and paying less than the minimum wage violates the dignity of labor.
The Exemption Act was declared unconstitutional.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The State must pay statutory minimum wages even for drought/famine relief public works.
2. Exempting relief works from minimum wage laws violates Article 23 (Forced Labor).
3. Poverty and starvation do not justify the State exploiting labor at sub-minimum rates.

cases.title: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. K.V. Shramik Sangh
cases.facts:
The Municipal Corporation engaged contractors to supply workers for sweeping and scavenging
streets. The Union of contract workers filed a writ petition demanding abolition of the contract labor
system and absorption of the workers as permanent municipal employees. The High Court directed
the Corporation to absorb them, holding the contracts were a sham to evade labor laws.
cases.issues:
1. Can a High Court under Article 226 order the absorption of contract laborers?
2. How is a 'sham' contract determined in the public sector?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The Union argued that sweeping and scavenging are perennial, core functions of a municipality.
Engaging contract labor for core civic duties is a blatant mechanism to deny them equal pay and
permanent status.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The Corporation argued that under the SAIL judgment, absorption cannot be ordered automatically.
They also argued that the High Court in a writ petition cannot decide disputed questions of fact
regarding whether the contract is a sham.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's absorption order, remanding the matter to the
Industrial Tribunal for proper factual adjudication.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the principles laid down in the SAIL judgment. It held that the High Court
overstepped its jurisdiction under Article 226. Determining whether a contract is genuine or a 'sham/
camouflage' requires detailed examination of evidence (e.g., who pays the salary, who exercises
disciplinary control, who controls the work). Such factual disputes must be adjudicated by an
Industrial Tribunal under the IDA, not by a High Court in a writ petition. While scavenging is indeed
a perennial municipal function, the legal route to absorption requires the workers to first prove the
contract is a sham in the proper labor forum.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. High Courts should not directly order absorption of contract labor under Article 226 if facts
are disputed.
2. Proving a contract is a 'sham' is a question of fact requiring evidence before an Industrial
Tribunal.
3. Core, perennial functions shouldn't ideally use contract labor, but legal procedures must be
followed for regularization.

cases.title: D.N. Banerji v. P.R. Mukherjee (Budge Budge Municipality)
cases.facts:
Two employees (a Sanitary Inspector and a Head Clerk) of the Budge Budge Municipality were
suspended and later dismissed for negligence and insubordination. The Municipal Workers' Union
raised an industrial dispute. The Municipality sought a writ to quash the proceedings, arguing that a
municipality, being a local government body, is not an 'industry', and a dispute with its
administrative staff is not an 'industrial dispute' under the IDA.
cases.issues:
1. Does a Municipality performing local government functions qualify as an 'industry' under the
Industrial Disputes Act?
2. Are disputes involving municipal employees 'industrial disputes'?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The Municipality argued it is a statutory body discharging local self-government duties, supported
by taxation, not a profit-making business or trade. Hence, the IDA does not apply.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The employees argued that municipalities undertake services like sanitation, lighting, and water
supply, which are essentially akin to business activities if performed by a private entity.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court ruled that Municipalities are 'industries' regarding their non-sovereign
functions.
cases.reasoning:
In this early, foundational case, the Court looked past the strict, traditional definitions of 'trade' and
'business'. The Court noted that municipalities undertake many functions-like supplying water,
generating electricity, maintaining transport, and sanitation-that could very well be done by private
commercial enterprises. Therefore, the relationship between the municipality and the employees in
these departments is an industrial relationship. The Court held that the IDA applies to municipal
workers, ensuring they have access to tribunals rather than having to strike and paralyze civic life.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A Municipality is considered an 'industry' under the IDA for its civic/utility services.
2. The source of funding (taxation vs. profit) does not disqualify an entity from being an
industry.
3. Laid the conceptual groundwork for the broader interpretation seen later in Bangalore Water
Supply.

cases.title: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
cases.facts:
Bhanwari Devi, a social worker employed by the State of Rajasthan to campaign against child
marriage, was brutally gang-raped by local men angry at her efforts. The incident highlighted the
complete absence of any domestic law providing protection against sexual harassment at workplaces.
Several NGOs filed a PIL seeking the enforcement of fundamental rights for working women.
cases.issues:
1. Does sexual harassment at the workplace violate fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and
21?
2. In the absence of statutory law, can the Supreme Court lay down binding guidelines for
employers?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The petitioners argued that a safe working environment is a basic human right. Without safety, a
woman's right to practice any profession (Art 19(1)(g)) and right to life with dignity (Art 21) are
illusions.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The State did not oppose the petition but acknowledged the legislative vacuum and sought the
Court's guidance.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court defined sexual harassment and laid down the binding 'Vishaka
Guidelines' to be followed by all employers in India.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that gender equality includes protection from sexual harassment and the right to
work with dignity. Relying on the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination
Against Women (CEDAW), the Court invoked Article 32 to fill the legislative void. It declared that
sexual harassment is a violation of Articles 14, 15, and 21. The Court issued comprehensive
guidelines, making it mandatory for all employers (public and private) to establish internal complaint
committees, define harassment broadly, and provide a safe working environment. These guidelines
had the force of law under Article 141 until the Parliament finally passed the POSH Act in 2013.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Sexual harassment at work violates Articles 14 (Equality), 19(1)(g) (Profession), and 21 (Life
and Dignity).
2. Employers have a constitutional duty to provide a safe, harassment-free workplace.
3. International conventions can be integrated into domestic law to fill legislative gaps.

cases.title: Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate v. Management of Dimakuchi Tea Estate
cases.facts:
Dr. K.P . Banerjee, the Medical Officer of the tea estate, was dismissed by the management with a
month's salary in lieu of notice. The workers' union raised an industrial dispute regarding his
dismissal. The management argued that Dr. Banerjee, being a medical officer, was not a 'workman'
under Section 2(s) of the IDA. The Union argued that even if he wasn't a workman, Section 2(k)
defines an industrial dispute as a dispute connected with the employment of 'any person', and the
union could raise a dispute on his behalf.
cases.issues:
1. What is the scope of the phrase 'any person' in Section 2(k) of the IDA defining 'Industrial
Dispute'?
2. Can a union of workmen raise a dispute on behalf of someone who is NOT a 'workman'?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The Union relied on the literal interpretation of 'any person' in Section 2(k), arguing it gives them the
right to take up the cause of anyone employed in the industry, including officers, if it affects industrial
peace.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The management argued that 'any person' cannot mean literally anyone. It must be restricted to
people in whose employment conditions the workmen have a direct and substantial interest.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court ruled against the Union, giving a restricted interpretation to the phrase
'any person'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'any person' in Section 2(k) cannot be interpreted broadly to mean anyone in the
world. For a dispute to be an 'industrial dispute', the workmen raising it must have a direct,
substantial interest in the employment or non-employment of that person. The workmen and the
person must belong to the same class or have a strong community of interest. Since Dr. Banerjee was
a Medical Officer (management/supervisory category), he did not belong to the class of workmen.
The workmen had no direct interest in his employment terms. Therefore, they could not raise an
industrial dispute on his behalf.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. ' Any person' in Section 2(k) does not mean literally anyone; it requires a direct and substantial
interest from the workmen.
2. Workmen cannot raise an industrial dispute on behalf of a non-workman (like a manager or
officer).
3. There must be a 'community of interest' between the workmen raising the dispute and the
person whose cause is espoused.

cases.title: L. Robert D'Souza v. Executive Engineer, Southern Railway
cases.facts:
The appellant was a daily-rated casual laborer who had worked continuously for over 240 days. He
participated in a strike, and as a result, his name was struck off the muster rolls by the railway
authorities. The management argued that participating in a strike broke his 'continuous service', and
his removal was just an administrative action, not 'retrenchment'. He challenged his termination for
lacking notice and compensation under Section 25F of the IDA.
cases.issues:
1. Does participating in an illegal strike constitute a break in 'continuous service' under Section
25B of the IDA?
2. Does striking off a name from the muster roll amount to 'retrenchment'?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The workman argued that under Section 25B(1), unauthorized absence or a strike that is not illegal
does not break continuous service. Since he worked 240 days, he was entitled to Section 25F
protections.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The Railways argued that his unauthorized absence due to the strike severed the master-servant
relationship, resetting his continuous service clock, meaning he was not entitled to retrenchment
benefits.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the workman, holding that striking off his name was
illegal retrenchment.
cases.reasoning:
The Court examined the definition of 'continuous service' under Section 25B. The section explicitly
states that continuous service is not interrupted by sickness, authorized leave, or a strike which is not
illegal. The Court found that the Railways failed to prove the strike was illegal. Therefore, his
participation did not break his continuous service. Since he had completed 240 days of continuous
service in the preceding 12 months, removing his name from the muster roll squarely fell under the
broad definition of 'retrenchment' (termination for any reason whatsoever). As the Railways failed to
pay him the mandatory compensation under Section 25F before terminating him, the termination was
void and he was reinstated.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Striking a workman's name off the muster roll constitutes 'retrenchment'.
2. Participation in a strike (unless proven illegal) does not break 'continuous service' under
Section 25B.
3. Completion of 240 days mandates Section 25F compliance before any termination.

cases.title: J.K. Iron and Steel Co. Ltd. v. The Iron and Steel Mazdoor Union
cases.facts:
Due to a shortage of raw materials, the company laid off several workmen. The union raised an
industrial dispute regarding the retrenchment. The Adjudicator (Tribunal) ordered the reinstatement
of the workmen, but did so based purely on his own subjective notions of 'social justice' and 'fair
play', ignoring the strict legal rights of the employer under the standing orders and the factual
economic constraints of the company.
cases.issues:
1. Are Industrial Tribunals bound by law and evidence, or can they adjudicate purely on abstract
notions of 'social justice'?
2. What are the limits of a Tribunal's discretion in deciding industrial disputes?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant / Management
The management argued that the Tribunal acted arbitrarily, ignoring the documented lack of raw
materials. They argued that 'social justice' does not mean overriding statutory laws or the employer's
bona fide right to organize his business.
B. Arguments for the Respondent / Workmen
The Union argued that Industrial Tribunals are not bound by the strict rules of civil courts and have
wide discretion to create new contracts and modify employer rights to protect workmen.
cases.judgment:
Result: The Supreme Court set aside the Tribunal's award, emphasizing that Tribunals cannot act as
benevolent despots.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the role of Industrial Tribunals. While it is true that Tribunals have wider powers
than civil courts-they can create new obligations and modify contracts in the interest of industrial
peace-they are not absolute dictators. Adjudication cannot be based on the subjective, abstract
whims of the adjudicator regarding 'social justice'. Social justice is not the fancy of an individual
judge; it must be founded on established legal principles, evidence, and a fair balancing of the
employer's economic rights and the employees' welfare. The Tribunal must act judicially, not
arbitrarily. Ignoring the employer's genuine economic inability to retain staff was a jurisdictional
error.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Industrial Tribunals must adjudicate based on evidence and law, not arbitrary notions of
'social justice'.
2. Tribunals have wide powers to modify contracts, but they must act judicially and fairly.
3. The employer's bona fide economic constraints cannot be ignored by Tribunals.

cases.title: Secretary, State of Karnataka v. Umadevi
cases.facts:
Various state departments and public sector entities had engaged thousands of workers on a daily-
wage, temporary, ad-hoc, and contractual basis for years. These workers approached High Courts and
the Supreme Court seeking 'regularization' of their employment, arguing that working for 10+ years
gave them a right to be absorbed permanently, relying on the 'equal pay for equal work' principle and
Article 21.
cases.issues:
1. Do temporary, ad-hoc, or daily-wage workers have a legal right to be regularized into
permanent government posts?
2. Does regularization of 'back-door entries' violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The State argued that regularizing temporary workers who bypassed the constitutional recruitment
process (public exams, advertisements) violates the fundamental right to equality of opportunity for
millions of eligible citizens.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The workers argued that keeping them on temporary rolls for decades, doing the same work as
permanent staff but paying them less and denying benefits, constituted unfair labor practice and
exploitation by the State.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A 5-judge Constitution Bench ruled against the automatic regularization of temporary/ad-
hoc workers, stating that 'back-door entries' cannot be regularized.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the State is bound by the constitutional scheme of public employment (Articles
14 and 16). Appointments must be made through a transparent, competitive process. Regularizing
workers who entered through the 'back door' (without public competition) deprives other qualified
citizens of their rights. The Court declared that a mere long period of temporary service does not
mature into a right for regularization. However, as a one-time exception, the Court permitted the
regularization of irregularly appointed workers who had worked for 10+ years without the protection
of court orders against duly sanctioned posts.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. No automatic right to regularization for temporary, daily-wage, or ad-hoc workers.
2. Public employment must strictly adhere to Articles 14 and 16; back-door entries are illegal.
3. The theory of 'legitimate expectation' does not apply to illegal temporary appointments.

cases.title: Hussainbhai v. Alath Factory Thezhilali Union
cases.facts:
Hussainbhai owned a factory manufacturing ropes. He engaged workers through independent
contractors. The contractors hired the workers, paid them, and exercised direct disciplinary control.
When the workers were denied rights under the Industrial Disputes Act, they raised a dispute against
Hussainbhai. He argued he had no master-servant relationship with them, as they were employed by
the contractors.
cases.issues:
1. Who is the true employer when workers are engaged through intermediary contractors?
2. What is the legal test to determine the employer-employee relationship to prevent evasion of
labor laws?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The factory owner argued that privity of contract existed only between the contractor and the
workmen. He merely paid the contractor for the finished product and had no direct legal connection
to the labor.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The Union argued that the contractor system was a sham to evade statutory labor welfare obligations.
Since the work was integral to Hussainbhai's business and performed on his premises, he was the
real employer.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court pierced the veil of the contract system, declaring Hussainbhai to be the
true employer of the workmen.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Krishna Iyer established the 'Economic Reality Test'. The Court held that the traditional test of
'control and supervision' is inadequate in modern industrial setups designed to evade labor laws.
The true test is economic control. If the workers are producing goods for the primary employer's
business, on his premises, using his machinery, and their economic livelihood depends entirely on his
business, then he is the real employer. The intermediary contractor is merely a device to camouflage
the actual relationship and strip workers of their statutory protections.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Established the 'Economic Reality Test' to determine the true employer.
2. Courts can pierce the veil of contract labor to uncover sham arrangements.
3. The principal employer cannot evade statutory obligations by interposing a middleman.

cases.title: Premier Automobiles Ltd. v. Kamlekar Shantaram Wadke
cases.facts:
A dispute arose between the management of Premier Automobiles and a segment of its workforce
represented by a minority union regarding the implementation of a settlement signed with the
recognized majority union. Instead of approaching the Industrial Tribunal under the Industrial
Disputes Act (IDA), the minority union filed a civil suit in the ordinary Civil Court seeking an
injunction against the implementation of the settlement.
cases.issues:
1. Does a Civil Court have jurisdiction to entertain a suit regarding an industrial dispute?
2. How is jurisdiction distributed between Civil Courts and Industrial Tribunals?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The management argued that the IDA provides a complete and self-contained machinery for
resolving industrial disputes. Therefore, the jurisdiction of ordinary Civil Courts is impliedly barred
under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The workmen argued that every citizen has a right to approach a civil court for the enforcement of
common law rights or to seek an injunction against a breach of contract.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court laid down definitive principles regarding jurisdiction, ruling that the
Civil Court had no jurisdiction in this specific matter.
cases.reasoning:
The Court formulated four clear principles: (1) If the dispute is not an 'industrial dispute' nor relates
to enforcement of any right under the IDA, the civil court has jurisdiction. (2) If the dispute arises out
of a right or liability under the general common law, the civil court has jurisdiction. (3) If the
industrial dispute relates to the enforcement of a right or obligation created strictly by the IDA, the
only remedy is the IDA machinery (Tribunals/Labour Courts). (4) If the right sought to be enforced is
a right created under the IDA (like challenging a settlement under the Act), the civil court has
absolutely no jurisdiction. The current dispute fell into category 3 and 4.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Civil Courts cannot adjudicate rights and obligations created exclusively by the Industrial
Disputes Act.
2. The IDA provides a self-contained machinery that impliedly bars civil court jurisdiction for
statutory industrial disputes.
3. Common law employment disputes (outside the IDA) can still be heard by Civil Courts.

cases.title: Jay Engineering Works Ltd. v. State of West Bengal
cases.facts:
In West Bengal, a militant form of labor protest known as 'Gherao' became rampant. 'Gherao'
involved workers physically surrounding the managers or executives of a company, locking them in
their offices, denying them food, water, or movement for hours or days, to coerce them into accepting
labor demands. The police, acting under a State Government circular, refused to intervene in these
Gheraos, calling them 'legitimate trade union activities'. The employers filed writ petitions
challenging the legality of Gheraos and the police inaction.
cases.issues:
1. Is 'Gherao' a legitimate weapon of collective bargaining and trade union activity protected by
law?
2. Does a Gherao amount to a criminal offense (wrongful confinement)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employers argued that Gherao is nothing but organized physical violence, wrongful
confinement, and criminal intimidation. They argued that the State Government's circular instructing
police not to intervene was a breakdown of constitutional machinery.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The Unions and the State argued that Gherao was a peaceful, democratic expression of collective
bargaining, akin to a strike or picketing, and protected under the Trade Unions Act.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A Special Bench of the Calcutta High Court declared 'Gherao' entirely illegal and
unconstitutional, quashing the State's circular.
cases.reasoning:
The High Court delivered a scathing judgment, ruling that 'Gherao' involves physical restraint,
wrongful confinement, and criminal intimidation, which are serious offenses under the Indian Penal
Code. The Trade Unions Act grants immunity to registered trade unions from civil suits for breach of
contract during strikes, but it grants absolutely zero immunity against criminal offenses. The Court
ruled that physical coercion and holding managers hostage is not collective bargaining; it is a crime.
The State Government's circular directing police to stand down was struck down as illegal, and police
were ordered to immediately rescue victims of Gherao.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. 'Gherao' is illegal and constitutes criminal offenses like wrongful confinement and
intimidation.
2. The Trade Unions Act provides no immunity against criminal acts or physical violence.
3. The State cannot instruct police to ignore criminal offenses under the guise of 'labor disputes'.

cases.title: Deepali Gundu Surwase v. Kranti Junior Adhyapak Mahavidyalaya
cases.facts:
Deepali, a teacher, was suspended and later dismissed by the school management following a
domestic inquiry. The School Tribunal found that the inquiry was highly defective, violated natural
justice, and that the charges were fabricated. The Tribunal ordered her reinstatement but denied her
'back wages' (salary for the period she was illegally kept out of work). She appealed, arguing that
since the dismissal was void ab initio, she was entitled to full back wages.
cases.issues:
1. Is a wrongfully dismissed employee automatically entitled to full back wages upon
reinstatement?
2. Who bears the burden of proof regarding whether the employee was 'gainfully employed'
elsewhere during the dismissal period?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employee argued that denying back wages penalizes the innocent victim of an illegal dismissal
and rewards the management for their vindictive and illegal action.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The management argued that 'no work, no pay' should apply, and back wages are not a right. They
argued the burden is on the employee to prove she was completely unemployed and starving during
that period.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the employee, restoring the principle of awarding full
back wages for illegal dismissals.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the jurisprudence on back wages. If an employer's action of termination is found
to be wholly illegal, void, or vindictive, the normal rule is that the employee must be restored to the
position they would have been in had the illegal action not occurred-which means reinstatement
with full back wages. The burden of proof initially lies on the employee to simply state on oath that
they were not gainfully employed elsewhere. Once they do so, the burden shifts entirely to the
employer to prove with concrete evidence that the employee was actually employed and earning an
adequate income elsewhere. Since the school management failed to prove she was employed, she was
awarded full back wages.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Reinstatement with full back wages is the normal rule if a dismissal is found to be illegal or
vindictive.
2. The employee must initially aver they were not gainfully employed; the burden then shifts to
the employer to prove otherwise.
3. Courts can reduce back wages only if there are exceptional circumstances or proof of
alternative income.

cases.title: U.B. Dutt & Co. v. Workmen
cases.facts:
The employer terminated the services of a workman under Rule 18(a) of the company's Certified
Standing Orders, which allowed the management to terminate an employee by giving one month's
notice or pay in lieu thereof, without assigning any reasons. The union raised an industrial dispute,
alleging that the termination was not a 'discharge simpliciter' but a colorable exercise of power to
victimize the worker for his union activities without holding a proper disciplinary inquiry.
cases.issues:
1. Can an employer use a clause in the Standing Orders to fire a workman without reasons
(discharge simpliciter) to avoid holding a domestic inquiry for misconduct?
2. Can Industrial Tribunals pierce the veil of a 'discharge simpliciter' to uncover victimization?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employer argued that the Standing Orders constitute a binding statutory contract. If the contract
explicitly grants the right to terminate with one month's notice, the Tribunal cannot interfere with the
employer's contractual right.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The workmen argued that the management was using the notice clause as a camouflage to bypass the
mandatory disciplinary procedure for misconduct, constituting an unfair labor practice.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled against the employer, holding that Industrial Tribunals can look
behind the stated reasons for termination.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that in industrial law, an employer cannot hide behind the camouflage of a 'discharge
simpliciter' (termination without cause). If the termination is challenged, the Industrial Tribunal has
the right and duty to pierce the veil and examine the true nature of the order. If the Tribunal finds
that the real reason for termination was misconduct or trade union victimization, and the employer
used the notice clause purely to avoid holding a fair domestic inquiry, the termination will be struck
down as a colorable exercise of power and an unfair labor practice. The strict doctrine of 'hire and
fire' under common law contract does not apply in industrial jurisprudence.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The doctrine of 'hire and fire' is heavily restricted in Indian industrial law.
2. Employers cannot use 'discharge simpliciter' clauses to bypass disciplinary inquiries for
misconduct.
3. Tribunals can pierce the veil of any termination to determine if it is a colorable exercise of
power or victimization.

cases.title: Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation v. Krishna Kant
cases.facts:
Several employees of the RSRTC (a statutory corporation) were dismissed for misconduct after
domestic inquiries. Instead of raising an industrial dispute under the IDA and going to the Labour
Court, the employees filed civil suits in ordinary Civil Courts seeking a declaration that their
dismissals were illegal because the inquiries violated the corporation's Standing Orders.
cases.issues:
1. Do Civil Courts have jurisdiction to hear employment disputes involving the violation of
Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act?
2. How does this case clarify the principles laid down in the Premier Automobiles case?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employees argued that Standing Orders are statutory in nature. A violation of statutory rules
gives them a common law right to seek a declaration in a civil court that the dismissal is null and
void.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The Corporation argued that Standing Orders are essentially the terms of employment defining the
industrial relationship. Disputes over dismissals are quintessential 'industrial disputes' under the
IDA, barring civil court jurisdiction.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that Civil Courts have no jurisdiction to entertain suits regarding
dismissals governed by Standing Orders and the IDA.
cases.reasoning:
The Court refined the Premier Automobiles principles. It held that the Industrial Employment
(Standing Orders) Act and the Industrial Disputes Act must be read together as a comprehensive
statutory scheme for resolving industrial disputes. A dispute concerning the dismissal of a workman,
whether based on a violation of natural justice or Standing Orders, is an 'industrial dispute'. The
policy of law is to resolve these disputes quickly through specialized Tribunals. Allowing civil suits
leads to decades of litigation and defeats the purpose of labor laws. The Court categorically held that
where the dispute involves rights created by the IDA or Standing Orders, the jurisdiction of the Civil
Court is entirely ousted.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Civil Courts lack jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes regarding the dismissal or retrenchment
of workmen.
2. Violations of Certified Standing Orders must be challenged before Industrial Tribunals, not
Civil Courts.
3. Reaffirmed the exclusivity of the IDA machinery for industrial disputes.

cases.title: Bharat Forge Co. Ltd. v. Uttam Manohar Nakate
cases.facts:
Uttam Nakate, a helper at Bharat Forge, was found fast asleep during his working hours. His past
record was extremely poor, with multiple warnings and suspensions for sleeping on duty and
absenteeism. Following a proper domestic inquiry, he was dismissed. The Labour Court found the
inquiry fair and the misconduct proved, but invoked Section 11A of the IDA to reduce the
punishment, forcing the company to reinstate him with 50% back wages, reasoning that dismissal
was too harsh.
cases.issues:
1. What are the limits of a Labour Court's discretion under Section 11A to interfere with the
punishment awarded by an employer?
2. Can sympathy for a worker justify reducing the penalty for gross misconduct like sleeping on
duty?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employer argued that sleeping on duty in a manufacturing plant is gross misconduct. Combined
with a terrible past record, the employer lost all confidence in the worker. The Labour Court's
interference was an arbitrary exercise of misplaced sympathy.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The workman argued that under Section 11A, the Labour Court has wide discretion to award lesser
punishments to prevent economic ruin of the worker's family.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court set aside the Labour Court's order and upheld the dismissal, ruling
against misplaced judicial sympathy.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a strong message on industrial discipline. It held that while Section 11A gives
Tribunals the power to interfere with punishments, this power is not absolute or unguided. It can
only be exercised if the punishment is 'shockingly disproportionate' to the offense. Sleeping on duty
is a serious offense that compromises safety and productivity. When coupled with a habitual pattern
of indiscipline, an employer is fully justified in dismissing the worker. The Court firmly stated that
Labour Courts cannot substitute their own punishment based on mere sympathy or misplaced
compassion. Industrial discipline cannot be compromised to protect a chronically errant employee.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Sleeping on duty, especially with a bad past record, is gross misconduct justifying dismissal.
2. The power under Section 11A must be exercised judicially, not based on mere sympathy or
charity.
3. Courts will not interfere with disciplinary actions unless the punishment is shockingly
disproportionate.

cases.title: Balwant Rai Saluja v. Air India Ltd.
cases.facts:
The workers were employed in a statutory canteen operated for Air India employees. Air India was
required by the Factories Act to provide a canteen, but it handed over the operation of the canteen to
an independent contractor (a cooperative society). The canteen workers demanded that they be
absorbed as regular employees of Air India, arguing that since the canteen was a statutory
requirement for Air India, Air India was their principal employer.
cases.issues:
1. Are workers employed in a statutory canteen run by a contractor automatically deemed to be
regular employees of the principal employer?
2. What is the test to determine if the corporate veil should be pierced in such contract labor
arrangements?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The workers argued that running the canteen was a statutory duty of Air India. Air India provided
the premises, equipment, and subsidies. Therefore, the contractor was just a sham, and Air India was
the true employer.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
Air India argued that the cooperative society hired the workers, paid their wages, managed their
leaves, and held disciplinary control. Air India had no administrative control over them.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled against the workers, holding they were employees of the
contractor, not Air India.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the law regarding statutory canteens. Merely because a company is statutorily
obliged to provide a canteen does not automatically make the canteen staff its direct employees. The
Court applied an updated 'Control Test'. To determine the true employer, the court must see who
exercises 'complete administrative control'-who has the power to appoint, dismiss, pay wages, and
take disciplinary action. In this case, the cooperative society handled all these functions. Air India
only ensured the facility existed. Since Air India did not exercise direct administrative control, the
contract was not a sham, and the workers could not be forced upon Air India as regular employees.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Employment in a statutory canteen run by a contractor does not automatically make the
workers direct employees of the principal employer.
2. The 'complete administrative control' test (hiring, firing, paying) determines the true
employer.
3. Piercing the veil requires proof that the contract is a deliberate sham to evade labor laws.

cases.title: Workmen of Associated Rubber Industry Ltd. v. Associated Rubber Industry Ltd.
cases.facts:
The Associated Rubber Industry Ltd. purchased shares in another company and earned substantial
dividends. Under the Payment of Bonus Act, these dividends formed part of the company's gross
profits, increasing the bonus payable to its workmen. To avoid paying this higher bonus, the company
created a wholly-owned subsidiary 'dummy' company, transferred the shares to this dummy
company, and stripped the dividend income from its own balance sheet. As a result, the workers'
bonus drastically dropped.
cases.issues:
1. Can a company create a subsidiary entity solely to siphon off profits and reduce the bonus
payable to workmen?
2. Can the Industrial Tribunal pierce the corporate veil to calculate the true gross profits for bonus
computation?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The workmen argued that the subsidiary was a fraudulent scheme, a mere alter ego of the principal
company, created exclusively to defeat their statutory right to a bonus.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The management argued that under company law, a subsidiary is a distinct legal entity. The profits of
the subsidiary cannot be merged with the principal company to calculate the bonus under the strict
provisions of the Bonus Act.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the workmen, piercing the corporate veil to merge the
profits for bonus calculation.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that while a company is a separate legal entity, this principle cannot be used as an
engine of fraud or to evade statutory welfare obligations. It is the duty of the courts to pierce the
corporate veil if an ingenious device or dummy corporation is created strictly to defraud workers or
avoid paying a statutory bonus. The Court found that the subsidiary had no other business, no assets
other than the transferred shares, and no purpose other than diverting profits. The Court collapsed
the two entities, added the dividends back to the principal company's gross profits, and ordered the
payment of the rightful bonus.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Industrial Tribunals and Courts can pierce the corporate veil to prevent the evasion of labor
welfare legislations.
2. Dummy corporations created to siphon profits and reduce worker bonuses will be
disregarded.
3. Statutory rights of workmen cannot be defeated by clever corporate accounting or structuring.

cases.title: R.S. Ruikar v. Emperor
cases.facts:
R.S. Ruikar, a prominent trade union leader, led a strike of textile workers in Nagpur. During the
strike, he gave fiery speeches inciting the workers to physically picket the mill gates and forcefully
prevent 'blacklegs' (replacement workers) from entering the factory. He was arrested and charged
with criminal conspiracy and abetment of offenses under the criminal law.
cases.issues:
1. Does the Trade Unions Act, 1926 grant immunity to union leaders for inciting physical
obstruction and criminal acts during a strike?
2. Is aggressive picketing that blocks access to a workplace a legitimate trade union right?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
Ruikar argued that picketing is a recognized method of trade union protest worldwide. He claimed
immunity under Section 17 and 18 of the Trade Unions Act, which protect union members from
criminal conspiracy and civil suits regarding acts in furtherance of a trade dispute.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The Crown (Prosecution) argued that the Trade Unions Act protects peaceful persuasion, not physical
violence, intimidation, or preventing citizens from exercising their right to work.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Nagpur High Court upheld Ruikar's conviction, drawing a sharp line between peaceful
picketing and criminal coercion.
cases.reasoning:
This historic pre-independence case established fundamental boundaries for trade union actions. The
Court held that the Trade Unions Act provides immunity for agreements to advance labor interests,
even if they result in a breach of contract (e.g., calling a strike). However, this immunity does not
extend to agreements to commit offenses against the general criminal law. Peaceful picketing-
standing and conveying information or peacefully persuading others not to work-is legal. But
physical obstruction, intimidation, violence, or forming a human barricade to prevent others from
entering a mill constitutes a criminal offense. Inciting such acts makes a union leader liable for
criminal abetment.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The Trade Unions Act does not grant immunity for committing or abetting criminal offenses.
2. Peaceful picketing is legal; violent picketing or physical obstruction is a crime.
3. Trade union rights do not override the fundamental criminal law of the land.

cases.title: Rohtas Industries Ltd. v. Rohtas Industries Staff Union
cases.facts:
The workers of Rohtas Industries went on a massive, illegal strike. The company suffered immense
financial losses due to the halt in production. The dispute was referred to an arbitrator under Section
10A of the Industrial Disputes Act. The arbitrator found the strike to be illegal and directed the
striking workmen and their union to pay compensation to the management for the financial losses
caused by the illegal strike.
cases.issues:
1. Can an employer claim financial damages or compensation from a trade union or workmen for
losses incurred during an illegal strike?
2. Does an arbitrator under the IDA have the jurisdiction to award tortious damages for an illegal
strike?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employer argued that an illegal strike is a breach of contract and a tortious conspiracy. Just as
workers can claim wages, employers must have the right to claim damages for the illegal disruption
of business.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The Union argued that the IDA is a self-contained code. It prescribes specific penalties (prosecution)
for illegal strikes, but nowhere does it allow civil damages to be awarded against workers.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Union, quashing the arbitrator's award of
compensation to the employer.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Krishna Iyer delivered a landmark ruling protecting trade unions from financial ruin. The
Court held that an illegal strike is a creation of the Industrial Disputes Act. The Act itself prescribes
the remedy: criminal prosecution of the strikers and loss of wages. It deliberately does not provide for
civil compensation to the employer. If employers could sue unions for the millions of rupees lost
during a strike, the entire trade union movement would be financially crushed. The right to strike,
even if exercised illegally, belongs to the realm of industrial relations, not common law torts.
Therefore, neither a civil court nor an arbitrator can award damages against a union for organizing a
strike.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Employers cannot claim financial compensation or tort damages from workmen/unions for
losses caused by an illegal strike.
2. The remedies for an illegal strike are limited to those prescribed in the IDA (loss of wages,
disciplinary action, criminal prosecution).
3. Trade unions are protected from civil liability arising out of strike actions.

cases.title: Workmen of Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. Meenakshi Mills Ltd.
cases.facts:
Following the striking down of Section 25-O in the Excel Wear case, Parliament amended the
Industrial Disputes Act. Section 25N (requiring prior government permission for retrenchment of
workmen in large industries) was also challenged by employers. Meenakshi Mills applied to retrench
workers, but the government refused permission. The employers challenged the constitutional
validity of Section 25N, arguing it violated their right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g) by
forcing them to retain redundant labor.
cases.issues:
1. Is Section 25N of the IDA, which restricts an employer's right to retrench surplus labor,
constitutionally valid?
2. Does forcing an employer to seek prior permission before downsizing constitute an
unreasonable restriction on business?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employers argued that dictating how many workers a factory must employ, and preventing them
from shedding surplus staff during economic downturns, destroys the economic viability of the
business.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The State and Unions argued that retrenchment throws workers into destitution. The State must have
the power to independently verify if the retrenchment is genuinely for economic reasons or merely to
increase profits at the cost of human suffering.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of Section
25N.
cases.reasoning:
The Court distinguished this case from Excel Wear. While closing down a business completely is a
fundamental right, running a business while shedding labor is subject to greater regulation. The
Court held that Section 25N does not absolutely ban retrenchment; it merely regulates it. The
amended provision required the government to give reasons, allowed for an inquiry where both
parties could be heard, and provided a time limit. These safeguards cured the arbitrariness seen in
the old laws. The restriction on the employer's right is 'reasonable' and in the interest of the general
public to prevent unfair labor practices, mass unemployment, and industrial unrest. Balancing the
employer's right to trade against the workers' right to livelihood, the law was deemed valid.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 25N of the IDA (requiring prior permission for retrenchment) is constitutionally valid.
2. Restricting an employer's ability to retrench workers is a reasonable restriction under Article
19(6).
3. The State has the authority to verify the bona fides of economic downsizing.

cases.title: U.P. State Brassware Corpn. Ltd. v. Uday Narain Pandey
cases.facts:
Uday Narain Pandey was appointed on a temporary basis. His services were terminated without
following the procedure under Section 25F of the IDA. He challenged the termination, and the
Labour Court found the retrenchment illegal and ordered reinstatement with 100% full back wages.
The Corporation appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the enterprise was sick, closed down,
and could not afford back wages, and that the workman had not proven he was unemployed during
the intervening years.
cases.issues:
1. Is the award of 100% full back wages an automatic, inescapable consequence of a finding of
illegal retrenchment?
2. What factors must a Labour Court consider before calculating back wages?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employer argued that the rigid rule of 'automatic full back wages' is obsolete. The court must
consider the financial health of the employer, the nature of the employment (temporary), and the
delay in litigation.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The workman argued that since the termination was void ab initio, he is legally deemed to have been
in service continuously and is entitled to every penny he lost.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court set aside the order of full back wages, ruling that back wages are not an
automatic right but depend on facts and equity.
cases.reasoning:
The Court marked a paradigm shift in labor jurisprudence. It held that the old rule-where illegal
termination automatically led to 100% back wages-no longer applies mechanically. Industrial courts
