1. 'Employed in an industry' is not restricted to those directly involved in the core manufacturing or
commercial process.
2. Workers engaged in operations incidental or ancillary to the main business (like maintaining company
quarters) are 'workmen'.
3. The crucial test is whether the employment is by the industry for the purposes of its overall
organizational operations.

cases.title: Management of Kairbetta Estate, Kotagiri v. Rajamanickam
cases.facts:
Following violent altercations and an assault on the manager by some workmen, the management of Kairbetta
Estate closed the division, claiming they could not operate safely. They declared a 'lock-out'. The workers
approached the Labour Court arguing that this was actually a 'lay-off' under Section 2(kkk) of the IDA because
they were refused employment. If it was a lay-off, the workers were legally entitled to lay-off compensation
under Section 25C, which they demanded.
cases.issues:
1. What is the precise legal distinction between a 'Lay-off' and a 'Lock-out' under the Industrial
Disputes Act?
2. Are workers entitled to lay-off compensation if the employer shuts down operations due to violence
and indiscipline?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The management argued that the shutdown was a lock-out-a defensive measure taken in response to violent
intimidation by the workers. It was not due to a shortage of raw materials or economic reasons, hence it cannot
be a lay-off.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The workers argued that any refusal by the employer to give employment when the workers are willing to work
constitutes a lay-off under Section 2(kkk), triggering mandatory compensation.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the management, holding that the shutdown was a lock-out, not a
lay-off, and denied compensation.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clearly delineated the two concepts. A 'Lay-off' (Section 2(kkk)) occurs for specific, trade-related
reasons beyond the employer's control: shortage of coal, power, or raw materials, accumulation of stock, or
breakdown of machinery. It implies the employer wants to operate but cannot due to external economic/
physical constraints. A 'Lock-out' (Section 2(l)), on the other hand, is an employer's weapon of coercion or
defense during an industrial dispute. It is the temporary closure of the workplace by the employer due to a clash
of wills (like responding to a strike or worker violence). Since the Kairbetta shutdown was caused by worker
indiscipline and a hostile environment, not a shortage of materials, it was squarely a lock-out. Therefore, the
provisions for lay-off compensation did not apply.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A 'lay-off' is strictly caused by trade reasons (shortage of materials, power failure, etc.) as defined in
Section 2(kkk).
2. A 'lock-out' is a shutdown driven by an industrial dispute, coercion, or security concerns.
3. Workers cannot claim lay-off compensation if the factory is shut down due to a lock-out caused by
their own violence or indiscipline.

cases.title: Gujarat Electricity Board v. Hind Mazdoor Sabha
cases.facts:
The Gujarat Electricity Board engaged a large number of workers through contractors for tasks like coal
handling and cleaning. The Hind Mazdoor Sabha (union) filed a writ petition in the High Court seeking the
abolition of this contract labor system and directing the Board to absorb the workers as direct employees. The
Board argued that under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), only the
'Appropriate Government' has the power to abolish contract labor, not the courts.
cases.issues:
1. Do High Courts or Industrial Tribunals have the jurisdiction to order the abolition of contract labor?
2. Who is the competent authority to abolish contract labor under Section 10 of the CLRA Act?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The union argued that the courts possess sweeping powers to remedy unfair labor practices and exploitation,
and thus can order the abolition of the sham contract system.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The Board relied on Section 10 of the CLRA Act, which explicitly vests the power to prohibit contract labor in
any process or operation exclusively in the 'Appropriate Government' after consulting the Advisory Board.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that neither High Courts under Article 226 nor Industrial Tribunals have the
jurisdiction to abolish contract labor.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly interpreted the statutory scheme of the CLRA Act. It held that the legislature has exclusively
delegated the power to abolish contract labor to the Appropriate Government under Section 10. This requires a
specialized factual inquiry by an Advisory Board regarding whether the work is perennial, core to the industry,
and sufficient to employ full-time workmen. Since the statute designates a specific authority (the Government)
to make this decision, High Courts and Industrial Tribunals are entirely ousted from exercising this power. If
workers want contract labor abolished in an industry, their only remedy is to petition the Government. (Note:
The Court did clarify that if the workers claim the contract is a 'sham' or 'camouflage' from day one, an
Industrial Tribunal can adjudicate that specific factual dispute)..
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The power to abolish contract labor rests exclusively with the Appropriate Government under Section
10 of the CLRA Act.
2. High Courts and Industrial Tribunals have no jurisdiction to order the abolition of a genuine contract
labor system.
3. Industrial Tribunals can only intervene if the contract is alleged to be a fraudulent 'sham' to hide a
direct employer-employee relationship.

cases.title: Haldia Refinery Canteen Employees Union v. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd.
cases.facts:
Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) ran the Haldia Refinery, a massive facility covered by the Factories Act. Under
Section 46 of the Factories Act, IOC was statutorily obligated to maintain a canteen for its workers. IOC
engaged an independent contractor to run the canteen. The canteen workers filed a petition claiming that since
the canteen was a mandatory statutory requirement for the refinery to operate, they were automatically the
direct, regular employees of IOC, not the contractor.
cases.issues:
1. Does the statutory obligation of a principal employer to provide a canteen under the Factories Act
automatically make the contractor's canteen workers the direct employees of the principal employer?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The Union argued that the canteen was not an optional amenity but a core statutory duty of IOC. They relied on
earlier judgments (Parimal Chandra Raha) to argue that workers in statutory canteens are ipso facto (by
the very fact) employees of the principal establishment.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
IOC argued that it merely provided the building and subsidies. The contractor hired the workers, paid their
wages, managed their EPF/ESI, and held total disciplinary control. There was no direct privity of contract
between IOC and the canteen staff.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Indian Oil Corporation, holding that the canteen workers were
not its direct employees.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the complex jurisprudence surrounding statutory canteens. It held that merely because a
principal employer has a statutory duty to provide a facility (like a canteen) does not mean it must directly hire
the staff to run it. The employer is free to discharge this statutory duty by engaging an independent contractor.
To determine if the workers are direct employees, the test is not the statutory nature of the canteen, but the
'Effective and Absolute Control' test. The Court found that the contractor had the power to appoint, dismiss,
pay, and supervise the workers. IOC merely exercised quality control over the food. Since IOC had no
administrative or disciplinary control over the workers, they remained employees of the contractor.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The statutory obligation to run a canteen does not ipso facto make the canteen workers direct
employees of the principal employer.
2. The true test of employment is who exercises effective and absolute administrative and disciplinary
control.
3. A principal employer can fulfill statutory duties through genuine independent contractors without
absorbing their labor.

cases.title: State of Haryana v. Piara Singh
cases.facts:
The State of Haryana had employed thousands of workers on an ad-hoc, daily-wage, and work-charged basis
across various departments for several years. To address their insecure status, the State issued regularization
policies, but with conditions (e.g., minimum years of service). Many employees who did not meet the exact
criteria filed writ petitions. The High Court passed sweeping orders directing the State to blindly regularize all
ad-hoc employees who had completed just one year of service, overriding the State's specific policy criteria.
cases.issues:
1. Can the High Court issue blanket directives compelling the State to regularize temporary employees,
ignoring the State's own regularization policies and financial constraints?
2. What are the legal parameters for the regularization of ad-hoc employees?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The employees argued that exploiting workers on temporary contracts for years and keeping them in constant
fear of termination violates Articles 14 and 21. The High Court's order was a necessary measure for social
justice.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The State argued that regularization is an executive policy decision depending on vacancies, budget, and
seniority. The High Court cannot usurp executive functions and order blanket regularization of unqualified or
junior ad-hoc staff.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's sweeping orders, laying down comprehensive guidelines
for regularization while respecting executive policy.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the creation and abolition of posts, and the framing of regularization schemes, are core
executive functions. The High Court acted beyond its jurisdiction by ordering blanket regularization after just
one year of service. This forces the State to create unnecessary posts, bankrupting the exchequer and violating
the rights of candidates waiting in the employment exchange. However, the Court also rebuked the State for
keeping employees ad-hoc for years. The Court laid down guidelines: (1) Ad-hoc appointments should only be
a stop-gap measure; (2) An ad-hoc employee should not be replaced by another ad-hoc employee, but only by a
regularly selected candidate; (3) If a temporary employee has worked for a long time, the State should consider
them for regularization if a vacancy exists, relaxing age limits if necessary.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Courts cannot issue blanket orders for regularization overriding executive policies and sanctioned
posts.
2. An ad-hoc/temporary employee cannot be arbitrarily replaced by another ad-hoc employee.
3. The State must frame fair, structured policies to regularize long-serving temporary employees against
actual vacancies.

cases.title: Guest, Keen, Williams Pr. Ltd. v. P.J. Sterling
cases.facts:
The company had no fixed age of superannuation (retirement) when it originally hired a large number of its
workmen. Later, the company drafted and certified new Standing Orders under the Industrial Employment
(Standing Orders) Act, which introduced a mandatory retirement age of 55 years. Based on this new rule, the
company forced several old workmen to retire. The union raised an industrial dispute, arguing that the new rule
could not be applied retrospectively to workers who joined when there was no retirement age.
cases.issues:
1. Can an employer unilaterally introduce an age of superannuation through new Standing Orders and
apply it to existing employees?
2. What is the power of the Industrial Tribunal to modify certified Standing Orders to ensure fairness?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The management argued that once Standing Orders are certified by the statutory authority, they become the
binding terms of employment for all employees, past and future. They argued efficiency requires retiring aging
workers.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The workmen argued that applying a new, detrimental condition of service retrospectively alters their vested
contractual rights. Workers who joined expecting life-long employment (subject to fitness) were suddenly
thrown out.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that while the new superannuation rule was valid, applying it rigidly to prior
employees without a transition mechanism was unfair, and modified the retirement age.
cases.reasoning:
The Court struck a balance between the employer's need to modernize its workforce and the vested rights of the
employees. It held that while Certified Standing Orders are binding, Industrial Tribunals have the jurisdiction to
determine if their application in a specific case causes undue hardship or unfair labor practice. The Court found
that abruptly forcing workers to retire at 55 when they had joined without any such expectation was harsh and
inequitable. Using its adjudicatory powers, the Supreme Court modified the rule: For workmen who joined
before the Standing Orders were certified, the retirement age was raised to 60 years, providing them a fair
transitional cushion. For those who joined after, the rule of 55 years applied.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Certified Standing Orders govern the terms of employment, but their application must be fair and
equitable.
2. Drastic, detrimental changes in service conditions cannot be suddenly forced upon existing employees
who had different vested expectations.
3. Industrial Tribunals can modify the application of Standing Orders to prevent severe hardship to prior
employees.

cases.title: Pipraich Sugar Mills Ltd. v. Pipraich Sugar Mills Mazdoor Union
cases.facts:
The management of Pipraich Sugar Mills found it impossible to run the factory due to severe financial losses
and labor unrest. They sold the machinery and completely, bona fide, closed down the business. The workmen
demanded retrenchment compensation. (Note: This case occurred before Section 25FFF was added to the
IDA, which specifically deals with compensation upon closure). The employer argued that since the business
was dead and completely shut down, the employer-employee relationship was severed, and no 'industrial
dispute' could exist regarding a closed industry.
cases.issues:
1. Can an 'industrial dispute' be raised or adjudicated if the industry has been completely and genuinely
closed down?
2. Is the termination of services resulting from a bona fide closure of business equivalent to
'retrenchment' under Section 2(oo)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The employer argued that the Industrial Disputes Act is designed to settle disputes in a running industry to
ensure continued production. Once the industry is dead, the Act's machinery ceases to apply.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The Union argued that the workers were abruptly thrown into unemployment. The closure was essentially a
mass retrenchment, entitling them to compensation.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the employer, holding that termination due to bona fide closure is
not 'retrenchment' and the IDA does not apply to a dead industry.
cases.reasoning:
The Court made a critical distinction between Retrenchment and Closure. 'Retrenchment' means the discharge
of surplus labor in a continuing business. If a business is completely and genuinely closed down (not just a
temporary lockout), the entire employment structure collapses. The Court held that you cannot retrench a
worker from a business that no longer exists. Furthermore, the objective of the IDA is to maintain peace in
existing industries; it cannot breathe life into a dead one. Therefore, the termination of services on a genuine
closure is not 'retrenchment', and under the law as it stood then, the workers were not entitled to statutory
retrenchment compensation. (Historical Note: This perceived injustice led Parliament to immediately amend
the IDA and insert Section 25FFF, granting compensation even in cases of genuine closure)..
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Termination of services due to the genuine, total closure of an industry does not constitute
'retrenchment' under Section 2(oo).
2. (Pre-Amendment rule) The Industrial Disputes Act generally applies only to running industries, not
dead ones.
3. This judgment catalyzed the legislative insertion of Section 25FFF to protect workers during closures.

cases.title: Workmen of Food Corporation of India v. Food Corporation of India
cases.facts:
The Food Corporation of India (FCI) engaged hundreds of workers for handling food grains at its depots.
However, FCI engaged them through a complex web of contractors and cooperative societies. The workers
raised a dispute claiming that this contractor system was a complete sham; they worked exclusively at FCI
depots, handling FCI grain, under the supervision of FCI officers, year after year. They demanded direct
absorption into FCI.
cases.issues:
1. How does a Tribunal determine if a contract labor arrangement is genuine or a mere camouflage to
deny workers regular benefits?
2. Can the court pierce the veil and declare the workers as direct employees of the principal employer?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The workmen argued that the contractors were mere name-lenders. FCI exercised total control over their work,
attendance, and duties. The system was designed purely to exploit them and evade paying regular wages.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
FCI argued that it had no direct legal contract with the workers. The cooperative societies paid them, and thus,
privity of contract lay only with the societies.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court pierced the veil, declaring the contract a sham and ordering the absorption of the
workers as direct employees of FCI.
cases.reasoning:
The Court scrutinized the reality of the operations. It noted that the workers were performing the perennial,
core functions of FCI (handling grain at depots). The contractors had no independent establishment, no other
clients, and merely supplied manpower. Crucially, FCI officers supervised the work, dictated the hours, and
controlled the operations at the depots. The Court held that where the principal employer exercises dominant
control over the work and the contractor is merely a middleman introduced to deny workers their statutory
rights (like provident fund, regular pay scales), the contract is a camouflage. The Court tore the veil,
established a direct employer-employee relationship, and directed FCI to regularize the workers.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. If a principal employer exercises dominant control over the work of contract laborers performing
perennial core functions, the contract is a sham.
2. Courts will pierce the veil of a sham contract system designed to exploit labor.
3. Workers under a sham contract are legally the direct employees of the principal employer.

cases.title: U.P. Income Tax Department Contingent Paid Staff Welfare Association v. Union of India
cases.facts:
The Income Tax Department employed a large number of Class IV staff (peons, sweepers, watchmen) as
'contingent paid staff' on daily wages. They had been working continuously for years, performing the exact
same duties as regular Class IV employees in the department. However, they were paid meager daily wages and
denied all benefits like DA, HRA, and leave. The association filed a writ petition demanding regularization and
'equal pay for equal work'.
cases.issues:
1. Does the principle of 'equal pay for equal work' apply to contingent or daily-wage staff working in
government departments?
2. Can the government indefinitely exploit workers as 'contingent' staff for perennial work?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The Association argued that extracting the same work but paying vastly different wages violates Article 14 and
Article 39(d). Keeping them 'contingent' for years for permanent administrative work was a fraud on the
statute.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The Union of India argued that contingent staff are hired for casual, temporary needs without following the
strict recruitment rules. Paying them regular scales would circumvent the formal recruitment process.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the contingent staff, enforcing the principle of equal pay for equal
work.
cases.reasoning:
The Court expressed shock that a major government department was exploiting citizens by keeping them as
daily wagers for years for regular departmental work. The Court held that 'equal pay for equal work' is not an
abstract doctrine but a constitutional goal. If the contingent staff are doing the same work, under the same
employer, with the same responsibilities as the regular Class IV staff, the government cannot discriminate in
their pay simply by calling them 'contingent'. The Court directed the Government of India to immediately pay
them wages at the minimum of the pay scale applicable to regular Class IV employees and to frame a scheme
to absorb these workers permanently.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The principle of 'equal pay for equal work' applies forcefully to contingent/daily-wage staff doing
identical work as regular staff.
2. The Government cannot exploit workers by keeping them on daily wages for years to perform
perennial departmental functions.
3. Artificial labels like 'contingent' cannot justify discriminatory wage structures.

cases.title: Bharat Bank Ltd. v. Employees of Bharat Bank
cases.facts:
An industrial dispute between Bharat Bank and its employees was adjudicated by an Industrial Tribunal, which
passed an award in favor of the employees. The Bank sought to appeal the award directly to the Supreme Court
under Article 136 of the Constitution (Special Leave Petition). Article 136 allows the SC to grant leave to
appeal from any judgment or order made by any 'Court or Tribunal' in India. The employees raised a
preliminary objection, arguing that an Industrial Tribunal is an administrative/arbitral body, not a 'Court or
Tribunal' under Article 136.
cases.issues:
1. Is an Industrial Tribunal constituted under the Industrial Disputes Act considered a 'Tribunal' within
the meaning of Article 136 of the Constitution?
2. Can the Supreme Court entertain direct appeals against the awards of Industrial Tribunals?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The Bank argued that Industrial Tribunals exercise judicial functions, record evidence, hear parties, and deliver
binding judgments. Therefore, they fall squarely within the definition of a Tribunal under Article 136.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The employees argued that an Industrial Tribunal does not strictly follow civil law; it decides based on policy,
equity, and social justice. It acts more like an executive arbitrator than a judicial court.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A Constitution Bench held that an Industrial Tribunal is a 'Tribunal' under Article 136, giving the
Supreme Court jurisdiction to hear direct appeals.
cases.reasoning:
The Court analyzed the nature and functions of an Industrial Tribunal. While it is true that Tribunals are not
bound by the strict rules of evidence and can create new contracts (unlike civil courts), they are nevertheless
invested with the State's inherent judicial power. They are created by a statute, they adjudicate disputes
between parties, they have the power to summon witnesses and administer oaths, and their awards are binding
and enforceable by law. Because they possess all the 'trappings of a court' and exercise quasi-judicial functions,
they qualify as 'Tribunals' under Article 136. This landmark ruling opened the doors for the Supreme Court to
actively shape Indian labor jurisprudence.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Industrial Tribunals exercise quasi-judicial functions and possess the 'trappings of a court'.
2. They qualify as 'Tribunals' within the meaning of Article 136 of the Constitution.
3. The Supreme Court has the constitutional jurisdiction to entertain Special Leave Petitions against
Industrial Tribunal awards.

cases.title: Express Newspapers (Private) Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.facts:
The Parliament enacted the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act,
1955. Under this Act, a Wage Board was constituted to fix the rates of wages for journalists. The Wage Board
fixed significantly higher wage structures. Various newspaper establishments challenged the constitutional
validity of the Act and the Wage Board's decision, arguing that forcing them to pay these high wages without
assessing their financial capacity would bankrupt them, violating their freedom of press (Art 19(1)(a)) and right
to trade (Art 19(1)(g)).
cases.issues:
1. Is the Working Journalists Act constitutionally valid?
2. Can a Wage Board fix a 'fair wage' or 'living wage' without explicitly evaluating the employer's
financial 'capacity to pay'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The newspaper owners argued that the Wage Board arbitrarily hiked wages without examining whether the
newspapers had the revenue to sustain them. Forcing them into bankruptcy is a direct attack on the freedom of
the press.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The Union of India and journalists argued that the press must pay its workers fairly. A business that cannot pay
fair wages has no right to exploit intellectual labor.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Act but struck down the specific wage
decisions of the Wage Board for failing to consider the 'capacity to pay'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court laid down a fundamental rule of wage fixation. It reiterated the concepts of Minimum, Fair, and
Living wages. A 'bare minimum wage' must be paid regardless of the employer's financial capacity. However,
when a Wage Board attempts to fix a 'fair wage' (which is higher than the bare minimum), it is an absolute legal
requirement to assess the industry's 'capacity to pay'. The Wage Board must look at the profitability, reserves,
and future prospects of the employers. Since the Wage Board for journalists had arbitrarily fixed higher scales
without conducting a factual inquiry into the newspaper industry's financial capacity to bear the burden, their
specific decision was illegal and ultra vires.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Fixation of any wage structure above the 'bare minimum wage' (i.e., fair wages) requires a mandatory
assessment of the employer's capacity to pay.
2. The Working Journalists Act is a valid social welfare legislation and does not violate the freedom of the
press.
3. Wage Boards must act quasi-judicially and base their awards on economic realities.

cases.title: Greaves Cotton & Co. v. Their Workmen
cases.facts:
Greaves Cotton & Co. was a large enterprise managing several subsidiary companies. The workmen raised an
industrial dispute demanding a revision in their wage scales and Dearness Allowance (DA). The Industrial
Tribunal drastically revised the wage structure upwards, granting them the same pay scales as those prevailing
in massive, highly profitable multinational companies operating in the same region. Greaves Cotton appealed,
arguing they did not have the financial capacity to match those multinational giants.
cases.issues:
1. What is the correct methodology for Industrial Tribunals to fix or revise wage structures and Dearness
Allowance?
2. How should the 'Region-cum-Industry' formula be applied?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The management argued that the Tribunal wrongly compared them to companies that were vastly superior in
size, capital, and profitability. Wages must be fixed based on the specific company's financial capacity, not just
the geographical region.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The workmen argued that to prevent labor unrest and migration, workers doing the same type of job in the
same geographical region (Bombay) should get the same wages, regardless of the specific company.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court refined the 'Region-cum-Industry' formula, laying down the definitive rules for
wage fixation.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established that when fixing wage scales and DA, Tribunals must apply the 'Region-cum-Industry'
formula. This requires looking at the prevailing wages in comparable industries in the same geographical
region. However, the comparison cannot be blind. A Tribunal must compare 'like with like'. It must select a
cross-section of industries that are comparable in terms of: (1) Capital invested, (2) Extent of business/turnover,
(3) Profits, and (4) Nature of the business. Forcing a medium-sized company like Greaves Cotton to pay wages
identical to a massive multinational monopoly merely because they are in the same city is legally flawed. The
employer's specific 'capacity to pay' remains the paramount limiting factor.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Wage fixation must follow the 'Region-cum-Industry' formula.
2. The comparison must be with comparable units in the same region, based on size, capital, turnover, and
profits ('comparing like with like').
3. The individual employer's financial capacity to pay is the ultimate constraint in fixing fair wages.

cases.title: French Motor Car Co. Ltd. v. Workmen
cases.facts:
The workmen of French Motor Car Co., which operated a motor repair and service workshop, demanded a
revision of their wage scales. The Industrial Tribunal noted that the company was financially very prosperous.
However, when applying the 'Region-cum-Industry' formula, the Tribunal found no other motor repair
workshops of comparable size in the region. Consequently, the Tribunal compared their wages with those of
workers in totally different industries (like engineering and heavy manufacturing) in the same region and hiked
the wages.
cases.issues:
1. If there are no comparable industries in the same region, can a Tribunal compare wages with entirely
different industries to apply the Region-cum-Industry formula?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The management argued that comparing a motor repair shop with large-scale heavy engineering or chemical
factories is absurd. The nature of the work is entirely different, invalidating the award.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The workmen argued that since the company was highly profitable and no exact comparable industry existed
locally, the Tribunal had to look at the general wage levels of manual/clerical labor in the region to ensure a
decent standard of living.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court upheld the Tribunal's approach in this specific scenario, creating an exception to
the strict Region-cum-Industry rule.
cases.reasoning:
The Court nuanced its stance on wage fixation. The general rule is to compare 'like with like' within the same
industry in the same region. However, the Court held that where a company is a near-monopoly or is so large
that there are no comparable units in its specific industry within that region, the Tribunal cannot simply freeze
the workers' wages. In such exceptional cases, the Tribunal is justified in looking at the prevailing wages in
other industries in the same region that employ workers doing similar types of manual or clerical work.
Since French Motor Car Co. was highly prosperous and lacked direct regional peers, comparing their basic
labor wages with those of general engineering firms in the area was a valid exercise of industrial adjudication
to secure fair wages.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The general rule is to compare wages within the same industry and same region.
2. Exception: If an employer is a monopoly or lacks comparable peers in the region, wages can be
compared with different but broadly similar industries in that region.
3. A highly prosperous company cannot use the lack of direct competitors as an excuse to pay lower
wages.

cases.title: National Engineering Industries Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan
cases.facts:
A recognized trade union signed a comprehensive settlement with the management regarding wages and
service conditions. A minority, unrecognized rival union opposed the settlement. Instead of raising an industrial
dispute under the machinery of the Industrial Disputes Act, the rival union filed a Writ Petition under Article
226 in the High Court, challenging the legality of the settlement. The High Court entertained the writ and
stayed the settlement.
cases.issues:
1. Can a High Court entertain a writ petition under Article 226 regarding an industrial dispute when a
statutory remedy exists under the IDA?
2. Is a settlement signed by a recognized majority union binding on minority rival unions?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The management argued that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere. The IDA is a self-contained code.
If the minority union felt the settlement was fraudulent or illegal, they had to raise an industrial dispute and go
to the Tribunal, not bypass the statute via a writ.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The rival union argued that the settlement was a fraud on the workers and violated their fundamental rights,
justifying the invocation of the High Court's extraordinary writ jurisdiction.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court strongly rebuked the High Court, quashed the writ proceedings, and emphasized
the exhaustion of statutory remedies.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reiterated the strict boundaries of judicial interference in labor matters. The Industrial Disputes Act
provides a complete, specialized statutory framework for resolving disputes, including challenges to
settlements. The Supreme Court held that High Courts must not entertain writ petitions under Article 226 when
an effective, alternative statutory remedy is available under the IDA. Bypassing the Tribunal destroys the
mechanism of industrial adjudication. Furthermore, the Court noted that a settlement arrived at in the course of
conciliation proceedings with a recognized majority union is binding on all workmen. If a minority union
disputes it, it must prove mala fides before an Industrial Tribunal based on evidence, which cannot be done in
summary writ proceedings.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. High Courts should not entertain writ petitions (Article 226) in labor matters if an alternative statutory
remedy exists under the IDA.
2. The IDA is a self-contained code; disputes regarding settlements must be adjudicated by Industrial
Tribunals.
3. Settlements signed by recognized majority unions are generally binding to maintain industrial peace.

cases.title: Kamani Metals & Alloys Ltd. v. Their Workmen
cases.facts:
The workmen demanded a revision of their wage scales and Dearness Allowance, pointing out that the cost of
living had risen significantly, and the company was making huge profits. The company resisted, arguing that
they were already paying a 'fair wage' according to industry standards, and therefore they should not be forced
to increase wages just because they were profitable.
cases.issues:
1. Can a Tribunal revise wage scales upwards if the company is already paying a 'fair wage'?
2. Is the attainment of a 'living wage' a static or dynamic concept?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Management
The management argued that once an employer pays a fair wage matching the Region-cum-Industry standard,
its obligation is fulfilled. Forcing it to pay more penalizes its business efficiency and success.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Workmen
The workmen argued that their current wages barely covered necessities. As long as the wages have not
reached the ultimate standard of a 'living wage', and the company has the capacity to pay, the wages must be
revised upwards.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the workmen, directing the upward revision of wages to inch
closer to a living wage.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a philosophical exposition on the concept of wages. It held that the concept of a 'living
wage' is not static; it is dynamic and expands with the growth of the national economy and changing social
standards. The ultimate constitutional goal (Article 43) is to secure a living wage for all workers. Therefore, if a
company is highly prosperous and its current wage structure (even if it is a 'fair wage') falls short of a 'living
wage', the Industrial Tribunal is fully justified in revising the wages upwards. An employer cannot freeze wages
merely because they meet current regional averages, provided they have the financial capacity to pay more. The
surplus generated by the industry is a result of the joint effort of capital and labor, and labor is entitled to an
increasing share until a living wage is achieved.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The concept of a 'Living Wage' is dynamic and evolves with societal progress.
2. As long as current wages are below the living wage standard, Tribunals can revise them upwards if the
employer's financial capacity permits.
3. The goal of industrial adjudication is to progressively move wages from the 'minimum' to the 'living'
standard.

cases.title: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel
cases.facts:
Several government employees (including police officers and railway workers) participated in strikes, mass
agitations, and insubordination. Due to the volatile and intimidating atmosphere, the disciplinary authorities
found it practically impossible to hold regular departmental inquiries. Invoking Article 311(2)(b) and (c) of the
Constitution, the authorities summarily dismissed the employees without holding any inquiry or giving them a
right to be heard. The employees challenged these dismissals as a gross violation of natural justice.
cases.issues:
1. Is the summary dismissal of government employees without a departmental inquiry under Article
311(2) constitutionally valid?
2. Can the principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem) be entirely excluded in public employment
disciplinary actions?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employees argued that the right to a fair hearing is a fundamental part of Article 14. Bypassing the inquiry
gives arbitrary, dictatorial power to the authorities, allowing them to dismiss anyone under the guise of
'impracticability'.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The Union argued that Article 311(2) specifically contains constitutional exceptions. When holding an inquiry
is genuinely not reasonably practicable (due to violence/intimidation) or against state security, natural justice
must yield to public interest.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A 5-Judge Constitution Bench upheld the summary dismissals, validating the constitutional exceptions
to natural justice under Article 311(2).
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the principles of natural justice are not absolute; they can be expressly or impliedly
excluded by the Constitution or a statute. Article 311(2) lays down the general rule of holding an inquiry, but its
second proviso explicitly creates exceptions. When the disciplinary authority records in writing that it is 'not
reasonably practicable' to hold an inquiry (e.g., when witnesses are too terrified to testify due to a violent
strike), the constitutional exception is triggered. The Court ruled that public interest, national security, and
maintaining discipline in essential services override the individual right to a prior hearing. However, the
dismissed employee retains the right to challenge the 'impracticability' itself in a court/tribunal later.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Principles of natural justice can be excluded by explicit constitutional provisions like Article 311(2)
provisos.
2. Summary dismissal without an inquiry is valid if it is genuinely not reasonably practicable to hold one.
3. The subjective satisfaction of the authority regarding impracticability is subject to limited judicial
review.

cases.title: Apparel Export Promotion Council v. A.K. Chopra
cases.facts:
A.K. Chopra, an officer at the Council, tried to molest a subordinate female employee in the office and a hotel.
He repeatedly tried to sit close to her, touch her, and proposition her, though she successfully resisted and
escaped before any severe physical assault occurred. A departmental inquiry found him guilty of sexual
harassment and he was dismissed. The High Court reversed the dismissal, reasoning that since he merely 'tried'
to touch her and didn't actually commit physical molestation, his actions didn't amount to actionable sexual
harassment warranting dismissal.
cases.issues:
1. Does physical contact have to be completed for an act to constitute 'sexual harassment' at the
workplace?
2. What is the standard of proof required in domestic disciplinary inquiries for sexual harassment?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employer argued that the High Court's view was archaic. Creating a hostile, intimidating environment
through unwanted sexual advances constitutes sexual harassment, regardless of whether physical assault is
completed.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The employee argued that the findings of the inquiry were based on circumstantial evidence, and since the
'attempt' did not culminate in physical harm, dismissal was disproportionate.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court strongly reprimanded the High Court, overturned its decision, and upheld the
dismissal.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the High Court's narrow definition of sexual harassment was abhorrent. Sexual harassment
includes any unwelcome sexually determined behavior, such as physical contact, advances, sexually colored
remarks, or creating a hostile work environment. It does not require actual physical touch or assault. An attempt
to molest or proposition a female subordinate is a severe violation of her fundamental right to dignity under
Article 21. Furthermore, the Court clarified that in domestic inquiries, the strict criminal standard of 'proof
beyond reasonable doubt' does not apply. The standard is 'preponderance of probabilities'. The victim's
consistent testimony was sufficient to prove the misconduct.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Actual physical contact is not a prerequisite for establishing workplace sexual harassment.
2. In domestic inquiries, the standard of proof is 'preponderance of probabilities', not 'beyond reasonable
doubt'.
3. Courts must not show misplaced sympathy to perpetrators of sexual harassment by reducing their
disciplinary penalties.

cases.title: Kameshwar Prasad v. State of Bihar
cases.facts:
The State of Bihar introduced Rule 4A into the Bihar Government Servants' Conduct Rules. This rule stated
that no government servant shall participate in any demonstration or resort to any form of strike in connection
with any matter pertaining to his conditions of service. Government servants challenged this rule, arguing it
completely destroyed their fundamental rights to freedom of speech and expression and to form associations.
cases.issues:
1. Is a rule prohibiting government servants from participating in demonstrations constitutionally valid
under Article 19(1)(a) and (b)?
2. Does the right to form associations (Article 19(1)(c)) include the right to strike?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employees argued that joining government service does not strip a citizen of their fundamental
constitutional rights. A blanket ban on all 'demonstrations' violates their freedom of speech and assembly.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The State argued that government servants form a special class. Maintaining administrative discipline and
uninterrupted public service justifies strict restrictions on their conduct under Article 19(2) & (3).
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court struck down the rule partially: it upheld the ban on strikes but struck down the
blanket ban on all demonstrations.
cases.reasoning:
The Court made a vital distinction between strikes and demonstrations. It definitively held that there is no
fundamental right to strike under Article 19. Therefore, the part of Rule 4A banning strikes was completely
valid. However, 'demonstration' is a much broader term. A peaceful demonstration is a form of expressing
grievances and falls squarely within the freedom of speech (19(1)(a)) and peaceful assembly (19(1)(b)). Since
Rule 4A imposed a blanket ban on all demonstrations-even innocent, peaceful ones held off-duty-it was
overly broad and failed the test of 'reasonable restrictions'. The Court struck down the word 'demonstration'
from the rule.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Government servants do not have a fundamental right to strike.
2. Government servants retain fundamental rights to free speech and peaceful assembly (demonstrations).
3. Blanket bans on all forms of peaceful demonstrations by civil servants are unconstitutional.

cases.title: O.K. Ghosh v. E.X. Joseph
cases.facts:
E.X. Joseph, a government servant, was the Secretary of a recognized Civil Servants' Association. The
Government later withdrew the recognition of the Association. Under Rule 4B of the Central Civil Services
(Conduct) Rules, a government servant was prohibited from joining or continuing to be a member of an
association that was not recognized by the Government. Joseph continued his union activities and was
subjected to disciplinary action. He challenged the constitutional validity of Rule 4B.
cases.issues:
1. Can the government make employment conditional upon an employee not joining an unrecognized
association?
2. Does Rule 4B violate the fundamental right to form associations under Article 19(1)(c)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employee argued that Article 19(1)(c) grants every citizen the right to form associations. Making this right
contingent on the subjective, discretionary 'recognition' by the government destroys the fundamental right.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The Government argued that Rule 4B is necessary to maintain discipline and ensure that government servants
do not join subversive or politically motivated organizations, constituting a reasonable restriction.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court struck down Rule 4B of the Conduct Rules as unconstitutional.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the right to form associations or unions is a guaranteed fundamental right. While the State
can impose 'reasonable restrictions' in the interest of public order or morality, Rule 4B went far beyond that. By
forcing an employee to leave an association merely because the government unilaterally decides to withdraw its
'recognition', the rule placed the fundamental right entirely at the mercy of executive discretion. The Court
noted that an association might be perfectly peaceful and lawful, yet lose recognition due to administrative
friction. Penalizing membership in a lawful association violates Article 19(1)(c).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The right to form and join associations is a fundamental right applicable to government servants.
2. Making government employment contingent upon joining only 'recognized' associations is
unconstitutional.
3. Executive recognition cannot be the prerequisite for exercising Article 19(1)(c) rights.

cases.title: Workmen of American Express International Banking Corp. v. Management
cases.facts:
The bank terminated the services of a temporary workman. The workman claimed that his termination
amounted to retrenchment under Section 25F of the IDA. To get the protection of Section 25F, a workman must
prove 'continuous service for not less than one year' (defined as 240 days of actual work in the preceding 12
months). The bank argued that if you only count the exact days he physically worked, it totaled less than 240
days, so he was not protected. The workman argued that Sundays and paid holidays should be counted in the
240 days.
cases.issues:
1. How is '240 days of continuous service' calculated under Section 25B of the Industrial Disputes Act?
2. Should Sundays and paid public holidays be included in the calculation of 'actual days worked'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The workman argued that employment is a continuous contract. Even if he didn't physically work on a Sunday,
he was legally in service and paid for it. Excluding rest days defeats the welfare purpose of the IDA.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The management relied on a strict literal interpretation of Section 25B(2), which uses the phrase 'actually
worked under the employer'. They argued this means physical presence on the shop floor.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the workman, holding that Sundays and paid holidays must be
counted towards the 240 days.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the principle of beneficial construction to labor laws. It held that the expression 'actually
worked' cannot be interpreted in a hyper-literal, pedantic manner to exclude rest days. Under various labor
statutes (like the Shops and Establishments Act), an employee who works for six days is statutorily entitled to a
paid day of rest on the seventh day. It is a fiction of law that he is 'working' for the employer by taking
mandatory rest to recharge. Therefore, Sundays and paid holidays are legally deemed to be days 'actually
worked'. Including these days pushed the workman over the 240-day threshold, entitling him to Section 25F
protection.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. In calculating 240 days of continuous service, Sundays and paid public holidays must be included.
2. The phrase 'actually worked' does not merely mean physical attendance; it encompasses the continuous
legal relationship of employment.
3. Welfare legislations must be interpreted beneficially to expand, not constrict, workers' rights.

cases.title: Surendra Kumar Verma v. Central Government Industrial Tribunal
cases.facts:
Several workmen were terminated by their employer. They had completed 240 days of continuous service.
However, the employer did not pay them the mandatory retrenchment compensation or give them notice as
required strictly by Section 25F of the IDA. The employer later argued that even if there was a technical
violation, the proper remedy was just to pay them the owed compensation amount, not to reinstate them.
cases.issues:
1. What is the legal consequence of retrenching a workman without complying with the mandatory
conditions of Section 25F of the IDA?
2. Does non-compliance render the termination void ab initio or merely irregular?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The workmen argued that Section 25F uses the mandatory word 'shall'. Non-payment of compensation
before termination makes the entire act of termination legally void, meaning they never legally lost their
jobs.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The employer argued that the failure to pay was an administrative error that could be cured by paying the
money later. Reinstatement imposes a disproportionate burden for a procedural lapse.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court held that termination in violation of Section 25F is void ab initio, resulting in
automatic reinstatement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a strict interpretation of Section 25F. The payment of retrenchment compensation and
notice pay are 'conditions precedent' to a valid retrenchment. This means the employer must fulfill these
financial obligations before or simultaneously with the termination. If an employer fails to do so, the
retrenchment is not merely irregular; it is void ab initio (invalid from the very beginning). Because the
termination has no legal effect, the workman is deemed to have never been terminated and continues to be in
service. The natural corollary is immediate reinstatement with full back wages. The employer cannot 'cure' the
defect by offering the money later.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Compliance with Section 25F (notice and compensation) is a mandatory condition precedent for valid
retrenchment.
2. Retrenchment without Section 25F compliance is void ab initio and legally non-existent.
3. The normal remedy for void retrenchment is reinstatement with full back wages.

cases.title: State of Gujarat v. Pratamsingh Narsinh Parmar
cases.facts:
A daily-wage worker challenged his termination before the Labour Court, claiming he had worked
continuously for 240 days and was thus entitled to the protections of Section 25F. He provided no documentary
evidence to support this claim, merely stating it on oath. The employer (the State) denied the claim, stating he
worked only intermittently. The Labour Court shifted the burden to the employer to prove the worker didn't
work 240 days and, when the employer failed to produce all records, ruled in favor of the workman.
cases.issues:
1. On whom does the initial burden of proof lie to establish '240 days of continuous service' in an
industrial dispute?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The workman argued that since the employer is the custodian of all attendance registers and muster rolls, the
burden should naturally fall on the employer to disprove the worker's claim.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The State argued that under the Indian Evidence Act, whoever approaches the court seeking a right must prove
the facts asserting that right. The initial burden must lie on the workman.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court set aside the Labour Court's award, ruling that the initial burden of proof lies
entirely on the workman.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified a crucial procedural rule in labor adjudication. It held that the burden of proof lies strictly
on the person who claims to have worked for 240 days. It is legally incorrect for a Labour Court to ask the
employer to prove the negative (i.e., that the workman did not work for 240 days). The workman must produce
some evidence-such as pay slips, appointment letters, or co-worker testimonies-to discharge this initial
burden. Only after the workman provides prima facie evidence does the burden shift to the employer to rebut it.
A mere self-serving affidavit by the workman, without any supporting evidence, is insufficient to shift the
burden.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The initial burden of proving 240 days of continuous service lies squarely on the workman.
2. The burden cannot be prematurely shifted to the employer to prove the negative.
3. A mere oral assertion or affidavit without corroborating evidence is insufficient to discharge this
burden.

cases.title: R.M. Yellatti v. Asst. Executive Engineer
cases.facts:
This case dealt with the practical difficulties workmen face in proving they worked 240 days, given the
precedent set in Pratamsingh Narsinh Parmar. The workman claimed he worked 240 days but had limited
documents because he was a daily wager. He formally applied to the Labour Court, asking it to direct the
management to produce the muster rolls and attendance registers. The management failed/refused to produce
the records. The question arose how the workman could discharge his burden when the employer suppresses
the evidence.
cases.issues:
1. How can a daily-wage workman legally discharge the burden of proving 240 days if the employer
holds all the records?
2. When can a Labour Court draw an 'adverse inference' against the management?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The workman argued that he did everything legally possible by demanding the records. Since the management
deliberately withheld them to defeat his claim, the court must presume he worked 240 days.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The management relied rigidly on the rule that the workman must prove his case and cannot rely on the
weakness of the management's defense.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the workman, explaining how the burden of proof can be
discharged and allowing adverse inferences.
cases.reasoning:
The Court fine-tuned the jurisprudence on the burden of proof. While the initial burden is on the workman, the
law does not demand the impossible. Since daily wagers rarely get formal appointment letters or continuous
pay slips, the Court held that the workman can discharge his burden by stepping into the witness box and
taking an oath, accompanied by whatever minimal documents he has (e.g., a few wage slips), AND by formally
calling upon the management to produce the official muster rolls. If the management then suppresses the
attendance registers or fails to produce them without valid reason, the Labour Court is fully justified in drawing
an 'adverse inference' against the employer under Section 114 of the Evidence Act. In such a scenario, the
workman's claim of 240 days is accepted as proven.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A workman can discharge the burden of proof by testifying and formally requesting the court to
summon the employer's records.
2. If the management fails to produce the demanded muster rolls, the Labour Court must draw an adverse
inference against the management.
3. This mechanism balances the strict burden of proof with the reality that employers control the
documentation.

cases.title: M/s. Parry & Co. Ltd. v. P.C. Pal
cases.facts:
M/s. Parry & Co. reorganized its business operations in Calcutta due to shifting commercial priorities, deciding
to close its engineering agency department and rely on different distribution methods. As a result of this
reorganization, a significant number of workmen became surplus. The company retrenched them after paying
statutory compensation. The workmen's union challenged the retrenchment, arguing that the company was
making huge profits overall and the reorganization was just a pretext to fire permanent employees.
cases.issues:
1. Does the management have a fundamental right to reorganize its business even if it leads to the
retrenchment of workmen?
2. Can an Industrial Tribunal interfere with a bona fide business reorganization on the grounds of
overall company profitability?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The management argued that deciding how to run a business, what departments to keep open, and how to
organize operations is an exclusive management prerogative. Tribunals cannot dictate business strategy.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The Union argued that retrenchment is only justified if the company is facing financial losses. Shedding labor
just to maximize already high profits constitutes an unfair labor practice and victimization.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the management, upholding their absolute right to reorganize the
business bona fide.
cases.reasoning:
The Court firmly protected the employer's managerial prerogative. It held that it is the exclusive right of the
management to decide how to run its business efficiently. If an employer decides to reorganize, rationalize, or
close a specific department for better economic management or strategic reasons, it is entirely within their
rights. The overall profitability of the company is irrelevant. An employer is not forced to run an inefficient or
unwanted department just because the rest of the company is making money. As long as the reorganization is
genuine and 'bona fide', and not a mere smokescreen to victimize active trade union members, the resulting
retrenchment of surplus labor is perfectly legal. The Tribunal cannot sit in judgment over the business wisdom
of the reorganization.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Reorganization and rationalization of a business are exclusive managerial prerogatives.
2. A bona fide reorganization that renders labor surplus justifies retrenchment, regardless of the
company's overall profitability.
3. Tribunals can only interfere if the reorganization is proven to be a mala fide sham to victimize workers.

cases.title: Niemla Textile Finishing Mills Ltd. v. The 2nd Punjab Industrial Tribunal
cases.facts:
Several employers, including Niemla Textile Mills, filed petitions challenging the constitutional validity of the
entire Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, particularly Section 10. Section 10 grants the 'Appropriate Government'
the discretionary power to decide whether to refer an industrial dispute to a Board, a Labour Court, or an
Industrial Tribunal. The employers argued that this gave the executive unchecked, arbitrary power to
discriminate between different employers.
cases.issues:
1. Is the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, constitutionally valid?
2. Does Section 10 of the IDA confer unguided, arbitrary, and discriminatory power to the Government
in violation of Article 14?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The employers argued that Section 10 provides no rules or guidelines on when the government should refer a
dispute or to which body. This unguided discretion violates the right to equality, as the government could refer
one employer to a Tribunal while refusing to refer another in a similar situation.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The State argued that industrial disputes are complex and volatile. Flexible executive discretion is necessary to
maintain industrial peace. The government must assess the specific facts, the severity of the strike, and the
public interest before making a reference.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Industrial
Disputes Act and Section 10.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the IDA does not violate Article 14. Section 10 does not confer absolute or arbitrary power;
the discretion is guided by the overarching purpose of the Act-which is to prevent strikes/lockouts and
promote industrial peace. The government is best positioned to evaluate the socio-economic and law-and-order
implications of a dispute. Sometimes, referring a trivial dispute might escalate tensions, while refusing to refer
a major one might cause riots. The choice between a Board, Labour Court, or Tribunal depends on the subject
matter and gravity of the dispute. Therefore, the delegation of this discretionary power to the executive is
reasonable, necessary, and constitutionally valid.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 is a constitutionally valid welfare legislation.
2. The power of the Government under Section 10 to refer disputes is discretionary but not arbitrary.
3. Executive discretion is guided by the underlying statutory objective of maintaining industrial peace.

cases.title: Indian Petrochemicals Corporation Ltd. v. Shramik Sena
cases.facts:
Indian Petrochemicals (IPCL) was statutorily mandated to maintain a canteen for its workers under the
Factories Act. IPCL engaged a contractor to run the canteen. The canteen workers filed a writ petition seeking
absorption as regular IPCL employees. While similar to the Haldia Refinery case, here the workers proved that
IPCL provided the premises, dictated the menu, heavily subsidized the meals, interviewed the canteen staff
before they were hired by the contractor, and integrated the canteen tightly into its operations.
cases.issues:
1. Under what specific factual matrix will workers in a statutory canteen be deemed direct employees of
the principal employer?
2. How does the court pierce the veil of the contractor in canteen operations?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The workers argued that the contractor was a mere figurehead. Since IPCL controlled everything from the
menu to approving the hiring of staff, and the canteen was a statutory requirement, they were de facto IPCL
employees.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
IPCL relied heavily on the general rule that statutory canteens run by contractors do not create direct
employment. They argued the contractor paid the wages and EPF.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the workers, declaring them to be direct employees of IPCL
based on the extensive control exercised.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified that there is no absolute rule that statutory canteen workers are never direct employees. It
depends entirely on the facts. The Court established a multi-factor test to pierce the veil: (1) Is the canteen
statutory? (2) Who provides the infrastructure? (3) Who exercises effective control over employment,
discipline, and daily tasks? In this specific case, the Court found that IPCL went far beyond mere quality
control. By interviewing the staff, heavily subsidizing the operations to the point where the contractor bore no
financial risk, and exercising pervasive administrative oversight, IPCL acted as the true employer. The
contractor was merely a camouflage to deny the workers IPCL's regular pay scales.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Canteen workers can be declared direct employees if the principal employer exercises pervasive
administrative and financial control.
2. Providing infrastructure, dictating hiring, and removing financial risk from the contractor indicates a
sham contract.
3. The 'Effective Control' test overrides the formal paperwork of the contractor.

cases.title: Mukand Ltd. v. Mukand Staff & Officers' Association
cases.facts:
A dispute arose regarding the revision of pay scales and allowances. The matter was referred to an Industrial
Tribunal. The union representing the employees presented a charter of demands. However, the union included
not only the 'workmen' but also the supervisory and managerial staff (non-workmen) in their demands. The
Industrial Tribunal proceeded to adjudicate and fix new pay scales for both the workmen and the non-workmen.
The management challenged the award.
cases.issues:
1. Does an Industrial Tribunal have the jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes and fix pay scales for
supervisory or managerial staff who are not 'workmen' under the IDA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The management argued that the Tribunal's jurisdiction under the IDA is strictly confined to 'industrial disputes'
concerning 'workmen'. Since supervisors and managers are expressly excluded from the definition of a
workman under Section 2(s), the Tribunal acted ultra vires by fixing their salaries.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The Union argued that the concept of an 'industrial dispute' under Section 2(k) includes a dispute connected
with the employment terms of 'any person'. Since the workmen had a community of interest with the lower-
level supervisory staff, the Tribunal could set their wages to maintain a unified salary structure.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court struck down the Tribunal's award regarding the non-workmen, strictly limiting the
Tribunal's jurisdiction.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the rule established in the Dimakuchi Tea Estate case but took it a step further regarding
direct wage fixation. The Court held that an Industrial Tribunal is a creature of the Industrial Disputes Act. Its
primary jurisdiction is to protect the rights of 'workmen'. While workmen can sometimes raise a dispute
regarding 'any person' if it directly affects their own employment conditions, a Tribunal absolutely does not
have the jurisdiction to directly adjudicate and dictate the pay scales, basic salaries, or service conditions of
managerial or supervisory staff. Fixing the salaries of non-workmen is an exclusive management prerogative
governed by ordinary contract law, completely outside the purview of the IDA.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Industrial Tribunals have no jurisdiction to fix pay scales or adjudicate service conditions for non-
workmen (managers/supervisors).
2. The IDA is designed exclusively for the protection and adjudication of 'workmen' as defined in Section
2(s).
3. Any award dictating the wages of non-workmen is ultra vires and void.

cases.title: Syed Yakoob v. K.S. Radhakrishnan
cases.facts:
Although originating from a transport authority dispute, this case became the bedrock precedent in labor law
regarding the scope of judicial review. An inferior tribunal passed an order based on its evaluation of facts and
evidence. A writ of certiorari was filed in the High Court to quash the tribunal's order. The High Court re-
examined the evidence, disagreed with the tribunal's factual conclusions, and quashed the order. The matter
reached the Supreme Court to determine the limits of a High Court's power over tribunals.
cases.issues:
1. What are the limits of the High Court's jurisdiction when issuing a writ of certiorari under Article 226
against the award of an Industrial Tribunal?
2. Can a High Court re-appreciate evidence and correct errors of fact made by a Tribunal?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The appellant argued that a writ of certiorari can only be issued for jurisdictional errors or errors of law
apparent on the face of the record, not to correct wrong factual decisions.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The respondent argued that if a Tribunal makes an incorrect finding of fact that leads to injustice, the High
Court must have the power to correct it under its supervisory writ jurisdiction.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court firmly restricted the scope of certiorari, ruling that High
Courts cannot act as appellate courts over Tribunals.
cases.reasoning:
The Court laid down the definitive boundaries for judicial review of tribunal awards. A writ of certiorari can
only be issued to correct errors of jurisdiction (acting without jurisdiction or exceeding it) or an error of law
apparent on the face of the record. It cannot be issued to correct an error of fact, no matter how grave. An
Industrial Tribunal is the final arbiter of facts. If the Tribunal has evaluated the evidence and reached a
conclusion, the High Court cannot re-weigh the evidence and substitute its own factual conclusion, even if the
High Court believes the Tribunal's decision was 'wrong'. The only exception is if the Tribunal's finding is
entirely 'perverse' (i.e., based on zero evidence).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. High Courts under Article 226 cannot act as appellate courts to re-appreciate evidence evaluated by
Industrial Tribunals.
2. A writ of certiorari is limited to correcting jurisdictional errors or patent errors of law.
3. Findings of fact by a Tribunal are final and immune from writ interference unless they are completely
perverse.

cases.title: Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. The Workmen
cases.facts:
The workmen of Alembic Chemical Works demanded an increase in their annual leave and sick leave. The
Industrial Tribunal granted the demand, standardizing the leave rules and significantly increasing the leave days
to match those offered by similar chemical industries in the region. The management challenged the award,
arguing that leave rules were already governed by the Factories Act and the Tribunal had no power to grant
more leave than the statutory minimum. They also argued 'res judicata', claiming a previous settlement had
frozen the leave structure.
cases.issues:
1. Can an Industrial Tribunal award leave benefits greater than the statutory minimum prescribed in the
Factories Act?
2. Does the principle of res judicata rigidly apply to industrial adjudication to freeze service conditions?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The management argued that the Factories Act provides a comprehensive code for worker holidays. Tribunals
cannot legislate higher benefits. Furthermore, previous settlements on leave should act as res judicata, barring
new demands.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The workmen argued that statutory laws only provide the 'bare minimum' floor. Tribunals have the power to
award fair and better conditions based on the company's prosperity and industry standards.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court upheld the Tribunal's award, allowing enhanced leave benefits and rejecting the
rigid application of res judicata.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that statutes like the Factories Act only prescribe the absolute minimum safety net. They do not
strip Industrial Tribunals of their jurisdiction to award higher or better leave privileges if the financial capacity
of the employer and regional industry standards justify it. Regarding res judicata, the Court made a crucial
observation: while the principle applies to prevent endless relitigation, it cannot be rigidly applied in industrial
law. Industrial relations are dynamic. Cost of living changes, companies grow more prosperous, and social
standards evolve. A settlement made a decade ago cannot permanently freeze the workers' rights. Therefore,
Tribunals can revise conditions if a material change in circumstances is proven.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Statutory labor laws generally provide a minimum baseline; Tribunals can award higher benefits based
on capacity and industry standards.
2. The strict civil doctrine of Res Judicata does not apply rigidly to industrial adjudication.
3. Changing economic circumstances and company prosperity justify the reopening and revision of
previous settlements/awards.

cases.title: Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. v. Workmen
cases.facts:
The workmen of Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. (HAL), a defense aerospace manufacturer, went on a sudden
strike. Because HAL was declared a 'Public Utility Service' under the IDA, Section 22 strictly prohibited
strikes without giving a mandatory 14-day prior notice to the employer. The workers failed to give this
statutory notice. The management declared the strike illegal and took disciplinary action. The workers argued
that their grievances were severe and immediate, justifying the sudden halt.
cases.issues:
1. Is a strike in a 'Public Utility Service' completely illegal if the mandatory 14-day notice under Section
22 of the IDA is not given?
2. Can the urgency or justice of the workers' demands excuse non-compliance with statutory notice
requirements?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The management argued that the law is absolute. In public utility services (like defense manufacturing, water,
electricity), sudden strikes paralyze the nation. Section 22 is a mandatory safeguard.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The workmen argued that the management's hostile actions provoked an immediate response, making the 14-
day wait impossible without surrendering their bargaining power.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that the strike was undeniably illegal due to the failure to comply with
Section 22.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly interpreted Section 22 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The legislature intentionally classified
certain industries as 'Public Utility Services' because a sudden halt in their operations causes immense hardship
to the general public and national security. To balance the workers' right to strike with public interest, the law
mandates a 14-day cooling-off/notice period. This gives the government time to initiate conciliation and
resolve the dispute peacefully. The Court held that this requirement is mandatory and absolute. The severity or
'justification' of the workers' demands is completely irrelevant if the procedural requirement is violated. A strike
without the 14-day notice in a public utility is void and illegal from its inception.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The 14-day notice requirement under Section 22 for strikes in a Public Utility Service is mandatory and
absolute.
2. Failure to give notice renders the strike automatically illegal, regardless of the merit of the workers'
demands.
3. The law prioritizes public interest and mandatory conciliation in essential services over immediate
union action.

cases.title: M/s. Avon Services Production Agencies v. Industrial Tribunal
cases.facts:
The company ran two distinct departments: a painting department and a packaging department. Due to
economic reasons, the company closed the painting department and retrenched its workers. The workers
challenged the retrenchment, arguing a violation of Section 25G of the IDA (the 'last come, first go' rule). They
claimed that instead of retrenching the painting staff, the company should have transferred them to the
packaging department and retrenched the most junior staff in the entire factory.
cases.issues:
1. How is the 'last come, first go' rule under Section 25G applied when an employer runs multiple
distinct departments?
2. Does the seniority list apply to the entire establishment as a whole, or is it restricted to the specific
department being downsized?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The management argued that the painting and packaging departments were functionally separate with distinct
skill sets. Seniority cannot be pooled across fundamentally different jobs.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The workmen argued that the establishment is one single entity under one management. Section 25G mandates
retrenching the juniormost employee in the entire establishment to protect senior workers.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the management, holding that Section 25G applies strictly within
the specific category or department of workmen.
cases.reasoning:
The Court provided practical clarity on the 'last come, first go' rule. Section 25G requires the employer to
retrench the workman who was the last person to be employed in that particular category of workmen. The
Court held that if a company has distinct departments requiring different skills (e.g., painters vs. packers, or
engineers vs. clerks), seniority cannot be pooled across the board. It is absurd to force an employer to fire a
junior accountant to save the job of a senior machine operator whose department is closing. The seniority pool
must be restricted to the specific class of workers doing identical or interchangeable work. Therefore,
retrenching the painters without touching the junior packers was legally valid.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The 'last come, first go' rule (Section 25G) applies only within a specific category of workmen
performing interchangeable duties.
2. Seniority is not pooled across distinct, functionally separate departments of an establishment.
3. Employers can retrench senior workers of a closed department without affecting junior workers in an
unrelated active department.

cases.title: Workmen of M/s Williamson Magor & Co. Ltd. v. Management
cases.facts:
The management of Williamson Magor & Co. promoted a junior clerk to a higher supervisory position,
bypassing a highly experienced and qualified senior clerk. The workmen's union raised an industrial dispute,
alleging that the supersession was arbitrary, unjustified, and an act of victimization because the senior clerk
was an active union member. The management challenged the Tribunal's jurisdiction to interfere, arguing that
promotion is an exclusive, unfettered managerial prerogative.
cases.issues:
1. Can the issue of 'promotion' and 'supersession' be the subject matter of an industrial dispute?
2. Under what circumstances can an Industrial Tribunal interfere with an employer's decision to
promote a junior employee over a senior one?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant / Union
The management argued that assessing merit and deciding whom to promote is the sole prerogative of the
employer. It is not an industrial dispute, and Tribunals cannot act as promotion boards.
B. Defendant / Respondent / Management
The union argued that arbitrary supersession violates service conditions, causes industrial unrest, and is often
used as a tool for unfair labor practice and victimization of union activists.
cases.judgment:
